subtitle: A Comprehensive Academic Study
description: An eighteen-module academic programme tracing the Christian faith from its foundations to advanced research — scripture, doctrine, history, practice and critical inquiry.
meta: 18 MODULES  ·  220 LECTURE TOPICS  ·  FOUNDATIONS TO ADVANCED RESEARCH
provenance: Reconstructed syllabus (18 modules / 220 numbered topics) authored for this engagement; the official curriculum file may be swapped in via ingest.py without re-authoring.

introduction.purpose: Christian Theology (theologia Christiana) is the disciplined, rational study of the faith as it is grounded in Scripture, shaped by the historical Church, and addressed to the whole of life. This programme is designed to equip students to articulate, examine and defend the central doctrines of the Christian faith with scholarly rigour and devotional seriousness.
introduction.scope: The curriculum spans the entire theological edifice: prolegomena and the nature of theological reflection; the doctrines of God, Christ, the Spirit, humanity and salvation; the person and mission of the Church; the Christian life and ethics; the history of Christian thought; apologetics and theology in conversation with modernity; and the methods of advanced theological research.
introduction.approach: Each module opens with a section divider, an introduction to the discipline, a sequence of numbered lecture topics, and a summary. Explanations distinguish biblical testimony, historical confession and systematic interpretation, and they present the major positions of different Christian traditions where they diverge.
objectives: Define the major doctrinal terms of Christian theology with precision and explain their biblical, historical and systematic context.
Trace the development of key doctrines from Scripture through the creeds, councils and confessions to contemporary expression.
Compare the major Christian traditions — Catholic, Orthodox, Reformed, Evangelical and others — with objective scholarly balance.
Apply theological reasoning to ethical, cultural and missional questions of the present age.
Demonstrate competence in the academic method of theological research, from problem formulation to thesis defence.

modules.title: Foundations of Christian Theology
modules.divider_intro: The meaning, nature, sources, method and purpose of Christian theological reflection.

intro.discipline: This module asks the threshold question that the whole programme rests upon: what is theology, and how is it properly done? It examines the word, its biblical and classical roots, the sources from which theology draws, and the method by which faith is rationally expounded.
intro.context: The study of theology begins with the conviction that God has spoken. From the early Church's 'sacred science' through the medieval university to the modern faculty of divinity, Christian theology has been understood as faith seeking understanding — reason in the service of revelation, not its rival.
intro.relevance: Every later doctrine stands or falls on the answers given here. The sources of theology, its method, its language and its relationship to philosophy and science determine how Scripture, doctrine and life are related throughout the course.
intro.focus: To define Christian theology precisely, locate its authoritative sources, and adopt the disciplined method that the remaining modules will employ.

topics.title: The Definition and Meaning of Theology
topics.explanation: The term 'theology' (theologia) is a Hellenistic coinage, used of the pagan gods by Homer, Plato and Plutarch. In the Christian sense it denotes the science of God as he has revealed himself in Scripture. Theologians have defined it variously as 'faith seeking understanding' (Anselm), the science of the triune God (Barth), and the rational exposition of Christian belief. The discipline is thus at once a science — ordered, systematic and critical — and a confession, because its subject is a living God who addresses his people.
concepts: Theologia: from theos (God) and logos (word, reason, discourse)
Theology as science and as confession of the living God
Fides quaerens intellectum — Anselm's guiding principle
The distinction between natural and revealed theology
topics.context: The word enters Christian use via the Greek Fathers; Origen's De Principiis (c. 215) is often cited as the earliest systematic work.
topics.takeaway: Christian theology is the disciplined, rational study of God as he has revealed himself — reason in the service of faith.

topics.title: The Sources of Christian Theology
topics.explanation: Historic Christian theology rests on sources that different traditions order differently. Scripture is affirmed by the whole Church as the inspired, authoritative norm (norma normans). The creeds and confessions stand as secondary rules of faith, summarising the Church's confession across the centuries. The living tradition of the Church's doctrine, worship and life, and the Spirit-witnessed experience of believers, complete the field. Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Reformed and Evangelical traditions weigh these sources differently, and an honest method makes the ordering explicit.
concepts: Scripture as the supreme, self-authenticating norm
Creeds and confessions as secondary rules of faith
Tradition as the transmission of the faith (traditio)
The experience of believers, illumined by the Spirit
topics.context: Westminster's 1646 confession makes Scripture the 'supreme judge'; the East stresses conciliar definition within the Church's life.
topics.takeaway: Theology must state its sources and their order; the traditions differ in weighting, not in inventing new authorities.

topics.title: The Nature and Method of Theological Reflection
topics.explanation: The classical method of theology proceeds from the biblical texts through careful exegesis, gathering the scattered testimony of Scripture on each theme, and articulating it in doctrinal language. The movement is descriptive (what the texts say), dialectical (how tensions are weighed) and constructive (the systematic statement), the whole being checked against the rule of faith and the confessions. Modern method additionally engages historical criticism, philosophy of religion and the social sciences as tools that serve — but do not govern — the theological task.
concepts: Exegesis precedes dogmatics: the texts before the system
The regula fidei as the test of interpretation
Analogia fidei — the whole of Scripture governs its parts
The interplay of text, tradition and situation
topics.context: Irenaeus developed the rule of faith against Gnosticism; the Reformers recovered 'Scripture interpreting Scripture'.
topics.takeaway: Sound method is circular in the best sense: text, tradition and situation check one another until confession coheres with revelation.

topics.title: The Relationship of Theology and Philosophy
topics.explanation: The relationship of theology to philosophy has long been a live question. The medieval maxim 'philosophy is the handmaid of theology' (ancilla theologiae) captured the classical view: philosophy supplies logic, categories and critique, while theology determines the content of belief. The tension surfaced in the thirteenth-century quarrel over the limits of reason and returned in modern debates about natural theology. A mature position affirms that reason is a gift of the Creator, indispensable to theology, yet subordinate to the reality of revelation.
concepts: Philosophy as ancilla theologiae — servant, not master
The use and abuse of reason in the study of God
Natural theology and its limits
The independence and the dependence of the two disciplines
topics.context: Aquinas synthesised Aristotle and faith; the Protestant Scholastics and later thinkers refined the boundaries of each.
topics.takeaway: Reason is a divinely given instrument of theology — valuable, universal, and rightly ordered beneath the authority of revelation.

topics.title: The Relationship of Theology and Science
topics.explanation: Theology and science address different questions from different vantage points: science describes the lawful, measurable order of nature, while theology interprets reality in the light of divine purpose and revelation. The two are not rivals so long as each respects the other's province. The great Christian scientists — Newton, Paley's predecessors, and the founders of modern research — saw their work as the study of God's book of nature. Conflicts, where they have arisen, have usually turned on over-reaching claims on either side, not on the methods themselves.
concepts: The two books of God: Scripture and nature
Complementarity: different questions, different methods
The dangers of scientism and of creationism
The Christian scientist as a model of integration
topics.context: The Galileo affair and the 'conflict thesis' are now historically nuanced; most scholars see a complex, mixed relationship.
topics.takeaway: Theology and science are complementary disciplines; each is at its best when it does not overstep its proper method.

topics.title: The Role of Faith and Reason in Theology
topics.explanation: Faith and reason are both human faculties, both created and both directed to truth, yet they differ in object and in mode. Reason discerns by evidence and logic; faith apprehends the person and the saving work of God by the Spirit's work on the heart. The Reformation slogan fides et ratio, and the older fides quaerens intellectum, both insist that the two are partners. Faith does not abandon reason; rather, faith supplies the content — revelation — that reason then expounds, defends and applies.
concepts: Faith and reason as distinct but cooperating faculties
Fides et ratio — the partnership of belief and thought
The noetic work of the Spirit in understanding
The danger of rationalism and of anti-intellectualism
topics.context: Aquinas balanced the two in the Summa; the Council of Faith and Reason (Fides et Ratio) reaffirmed the partnership in 1998.
topics.takeaway: Theology is neither blind faith nor cold reason, but reason rightly engaged with the truth that faith has received.

topics.title: The Language of Theology and Divine Predication
topics.explanation: How can finite language speak of an infinite God? Theology inherits a rich but difficult vocabulary. Predicates of God are understood affirmatively (we say what is of God), negatively (we say what God is not — the apophatic way), and analogically (we say what is of God by reference to creatures, while preserving the infinite difference). The doctrine of analogy (analogia entis) holds that our words are true of God not univocally (as of a creature) nor purely negatively, but by an analogy grounded in God's own self-communication.
concepts: The via affirmativa, negativa and eminente (supereminently)
Univocal, equivocal and analogical predication
The analogia entis and its critics
Mystery: the limits and the necessity of theological language
topics.context: Pseudo-Dionysius shaped the negative way; Aquinas systematised analogy; Barth challenged the analogia entis.
topics.takeaway: Theological language is genuinely true of God, but always by analogy — pointing to a reality that far exceeds every word.

topics.title: The Place of the Holy Spirit in Theological Study
topics.explanation: Christian theology is not merely an academic exercise; it is undertaken in the power and under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, who is the teacher of the Church. The Spirit who inspired the Scriptures illumines the mind of the student, guards against error, and applies the truth to the life of the believer and the Church. To study theology apart from the Spirit is to study the words of God without their author and their life-giving power. The discipline is therefore both an intellectual and a spiritual exercise, dependent on prayer, the Word, and the fellowship of the Church.
concepts: The Spirit as the teacher and illuminator of the Church
Inspiration and illumination: the Spirit's two works
The noetic effect of the fall on the study of God
Theology as a spiritual as well as an intellectual discipline
topics.context: The Reformers spoke of the 'inner witness' of the Spirit (testimonium Spiritus Sancti internum) as the ground of Scripture's authority.
topics.takeaway: The Holy Spirit is both the source and the guide of theology; to study apart from him is to approach God's Word without its life.

topics.title: The History of Theology as an Academic Discipline
topics.explanation: Theology developed as a distinct academic discipline gradually. In the early Church it was the 'first philosophy' of the bishop and the catechetical school; by the sixth century the great cathedral and monastic schools were training clergy. The rise of the universities in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries made theologia the queen of the sciences, crowned by the Summae of Aquinas and the great lectio systems. The Reformation re-founded the discipline on the principle of sola Scriptura, and the modern university inherited a rich, if sometimes contested, tradition.
concepts: Theology in the catechetical and monastic schools
The medieval university and theologia as queen of the sciences
The Reformation re-foundation on sola Scriptura
The modern university and the academic status of theology
topics.context: The Studium of Paris and the faculty of arts-to-theology structure shaped Western theological education for centuries.
topics.takeaway: Theology's academic status rests on a long history of formation, from the catechetical school to the modern university faculty.

topics.title: Theological Education and the Formation of Ministers
topics.explanation: The purpose of theological education is not merely the transmission of information but the formation of ministers who can think theologically, preach the Word, shepherd the flock, and defend the faith. The classical curriculum — the arts (philosophy, languages, history) followed by theology — trained the mind before it handled the mysteries. Formation is holistic, embracing intellect, character and piety, so that the minister is not a mere technician of doctrine but a mature servant of Christ, able to apply sound doctrine to the concrete situations of ministry.
concepts: Formation of mind, character and piety
The classical arts-then-theology curriculum
Competence in exegesis, homiletics and pastoral care
The minister as theologian, preacher and shepherd
topics.context: The seminary system matured after the Reformation; modern curricula balance academic rigour with practical ministry training.
topics.takeaway: Theological education forms whole ministers — competent in thought, mature in character, and devoted in piety to the work of the gospel.

topics.title: The Relationship of Theology to the Church and to Life
topics.explanation: Theology is not a free-floating speculation; it is the Church's own self-understanding and is accountable to the Church's confession and to the tasks of the Christian life. Doctrine is given not to be stored but to be lived. The Reformation insight that 'there is no Christian life without Christian doctrine, nor Christian doctrine without Christian life' captures the mutual implication. Theology therefore issues in worship, ethics, ministry and evangelism, and it is tested and shaped by the experience of the believing community.
concepts: Theology as the Church's self-understanding
Doctrine in the service of worship and ethics
The mutual implication of doctrine and life
The accountability of theology to the confessing community
topics.context: The 'sola' principles of the Reformation were grounded in the conviction that doctrine shapes the whole of Christian living.
topics.takeaway: Theology exists for the Church and for life; sound doctrine is the foundation of authentic worship, ethics and mission.

topics.title: The Nature, Sources and Aims of Theology in Summary
topics.explanation: This module has established the foundations on which the rest of the programme stands. Theology is the rational, systematic study of God as revealed; its supreme source is Scripture, supported by the creeds, tradition and experience in a clear order; its method moves from exegesis through articulation to confession, guided by the Holy Spirit and checked by the rule of faith. Its aim is not abstraction but the knowing of God, the building up of the Church, and the equipping of ministers and believers for the tasks of the Christian life. Every subsequent module applies these foundations to a specific region of doctrine.
concepts: Theology as the rational study of the self-revealing God
The ordered sources: Scripture, creed, tradition, experience
A method from text to confession under the Spirit
The aim: knowledge of God, the edification of the Church
topics.context: These foundations mirror the programme of the great theological Summae and the modern university course alike.
topics.takeaway: With the sources, method and aims of theology fixed, the programme turns to the supreme source itself: the Scriptures.

ideas: Theology is the science of God as revealed — reason serving faith, not replacing it.
Scripture is the supreme norm; the creeds, tradition and experience are subordinate witnesses in a clear order.
A disciplined method moves from exegesis through doctrinal articulation to confessional statement, guided by the Spirit.
summary.connections: The sources and method established here are the material and the instrument of every later module; they recur in biblical, systematic, historical and practical theology alike.
summary.progression: Having fixed the sources and method of theology, the programme turns to the supreme text itself: the Bible as the book of theology.

modules.title: The Bible: The Book of Theology
modules.divider_intro: The formation, inspiration, authority and interpretation of the Scriptures as the rule of the Christian faith.

intro.discipline: This module studies the Bible itself as the book of theology: its origin and formation in Israel and the Church, its claim to be the word of God, its canon, its transmission, and the principles by which it is to be read and applied.
intro.context: The Scriptures arose within the covenant communities of Israel and the Church, were recognised by those communities, and have been transmitted, translated and interpreted across twenty centuries. Their formation is thus both a divine and a human story — the Word accommodated to human language.
intro.relevance: If Scripture is the norm of all doctrine, then every other module stands or falls with the questions answered here: what the Bible is, why it is authoritative, and how it is to be read responsibly.
intro.focus: To understand the nature, authority and canonical structure of the Bible, and to adopt the principles of interpretation that the course will use throughout.

topics.title: The Origin and Composition of the Old Testament
topics.explanation: The Old Testament grew over centuries within Israel's covenant life: the Torah, the historical books, the wisdom and poetic literature, and the prophetic writings. The Hebrew canon — Law, Prophets and Writings (Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim) — was fixed in its present form around the time of the Council of Jamnia (c. AD 90), though its books were already recognised as Scripture within the community. The division into thirty-nine books corresponds to the Jewish threefold division, and the text was preserved with extraordinary care by the Masoretes.
concepts: Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim — the threefold Hebrew canon
Dictated, prophetic, wisdom and apostolic modes of composition
The canon as recognition, not creation, of Scripture
The Masoretic Text as the standard Hebrew witness
topics.context: The Septuagint (LXX), translated in Alexandria c. 250-150 BC, shaped the New Testament's quotation of the Old.
topics.takeaway: The Old Testament is a library of covenant history, recognised as Scripture by the faithful community of Israel.

topics.title: The Origin and Composition of the New Testament
topics.explanation: The New Testament arose in the decades following the resurrection: the Gospels and Acts, the Pauline and general epistles, and Revelation. The writings circulated among the churches, were read in worship alongside the Old Testament, and were collected into the fourfold Gospel and the complete canon. By the late fourth century — the Syntaxis of Athanasius (367) and the Councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) — the twenty-seven-book canon had achieved its final, universal shape on the basis of apostolicity, orthodoxy and catholic usage.
concepts: Apostolicity as the criterion of the New Testament
The fourfold Gospel: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John
The canonical process: recognition by the rule of faith
The Textus Receptus and the critical text
topics.context: The Muratorian Fragment (c. 170) and the lists of Athanasius, Tertullian and Eusebius trace the canon's emergence.
topics.takeaway: The New Testament canon is the Church's witness to the apostolic rule of faith — a library received and guarded, not issued from above.

topics.title: The Canon of Scripture
topics.explanation: The canon of Scripture is the list of books recognised as the inspired Word of God. The question is not how the books became canonical, but how the Church discerned which books were already so. The criteria were apostolicity or connection with the apostolic age, orthodoxy in content, and catholic usage in the churches' worship and teaching. The process was one of recognition, not conferral: the books did not become Scripture by the Church's vote, but the Church acknowledged what Scripture already was. Both the Old and New Testaments reached their closed form by the fourth century.
concepts: The canon as recognition, not conferral, of Scripture
Criteria: apostolicity, orthodoxy, catholic usage
The development of the Old and New canon lists
The closed canon and its practical consequences
topics.context: Athanasius's Easter letter of 367 gives the first complete list of the twenty-seven New Testament books.
topics.takeaway: The canon is closed because the apostolic witness is complete; the Church discerns and guards what God has already spoken.

topics.title: The Unity and Diversity of the Bible
topics.explanation: The Bible is a remarkable unity within a striking diversity: sixty-six books, by roughly forty authors, over about fifteen centuries, in two languages and many literary forms, yet bearing a single centre — the redemptive work of the one God in Christ. The diversity is no barrier to unity, for the authors were human and the Author was one. The progressive unfolding of redemption — promise in the Old Testament, accomplishment in the New — is a unity of fulfilment. This organic unity is the ground of the principle of Scripture interpreting Scripture.
concepts: One Author, many authors: the divine-human authorship
The unity of redemptive-historical fulfilment
Promise and fulfilment between the Testaments
The basis of the analogy of faith (analogia fidei)
topics.context: The 'canon within a canon' problem was solved historically by the principle of mutual illumination of the parts.
topics.takeaway: The Bible's diversity under one divine Author guarantees that its parts interpret, correct and complete one another.

topics.title: The Doctrine of Biblical Inspiration
topics.explanation: Inspiration asserts that the Scriptures are not merely religious literature but the very Word of God, written by human authors guided by the Holy Spirit so that what they wrote is God's word (2 Tim 3:16; 2 Pet 1:21). The doctrine is pneu-theopneustos — God-breathed — a statement about the origin of the text. The human element is real: the authors' styles, knowledge and situations appear throughout, yet the words are God's. Inspiration is verbal in the sense that the very words are given, and it extends to the autographs as they were originally written, the ground of the doctrines of inerrancy and infallibility.
concepts: Theopneustos: Scripture as 'God-breathed'
Verbal plenary inspiration and the human element
Inspiration of the autographs
The basis of inerrancy and infallibility
topics.context: The doctrine was formulated against Gnostic docetism and reasserted in the Reformation against the Council of Trent's view.
topics.takeaway: Inspiration is God's guarantee that the biblical authors wrote exactly what he intended them to write — human words that are divine words.

topics.title: The Authority of Scripture
topics.explanation: The authority of Scripture is its God-given right to command belief and obedience, resting ultimately on the authority of God himself, its Author. In the Reformed tradition this authority is self-authenticating: Scripture needs no external human authority to certify it, being attested internally by the Holy Spirit's witness to the believing heart (the internal witness of the Spirit). Its authority is comprehensive, extending to everything necessary for faith and life (2 Tim 3:16-17), and it is final in all matters of doctrine and conduct. The Church submits to Scripture, not the reverse; creed and tradition are subordinate witnesses.
concepts: Authority as God-given right to command belief and obedience
Self-authentication and the internal witness of the Spirit
The comprehensiveness of Scripture for faith and life
Scripture's final authority over creed and tradition
topics.context: The Reformation's sola Scriptura was a recovery of Scripture's final authority against the magisterial claims of tradition.
topics.takeaway: The authority of the Bible is the authority of God; it is self-authenticating, comprehensive in its scope, and final in all matters of faith.

topics.title: The Inerrancy and Infallibility of the Bible
topics.explanation: Infallibility means that Scripture, in the original autographs, is without error in what it affirms; it will not lead the reader into error in matters of faith and life. Inerrancy is the more precise modern formulation: the autographs are without error in all that they state, including history, science and prophecy, each passage being judged in its own literary category. The distinction between the autographs and later manuscripts — which contain scribal errors — is essential. The practical effect of the doctrine is confidence: the Word of God can be trusted wholly, and its teaching is the secure foundation of the Church's confession.
concepts: Infallibility: no error in what Scripture affirms
Inerrancy: no error in the autographs, all statements
The autograph-to-manuscript distinction
Literary categories and the interpretation of difficult texts
topics.context: The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978) is the most widely subscribed modern affirmation of the doctrine.
topics.takeaway: The Scripture God gave is without error in the originals; therefore the believer may trust the Bible wholly in faith and in fact.

topics.title: The Preservation and Transmission of the Text
topics.explanation: Although the original autographs no longer exist, the biblical text has been preserved with extraordinary fidelity. The Old Testament's Masoretic Text, with its system of vocalisation and marginal notes, and the discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls (1947) showed its accuracy to be remarkable. The New Testament is attested by some five thousand eight hundred Greek manuscripts and thousands more in other languages, so that its text can be reconstructed with a certainty unmatched in ancient literature. Copying errors occurred, but they are few, trivial, and none affects any doctrine of the faith.
concepts: The Masoretic Text and the Dead Sea Scrolls
The sheer volume of New Testament manuscripts
Textual criticism: the task of the editor
The preservation of doctrine amid textual variants
topics.context: The Qumran discovery (1947) confirmed the Masoretes' accuracy over a millennium of transmission.
topics.takeaway: The biblical text has been transmitted with remarkable fidelity; the doctrine of the faith stands secure on the evidence of the manuscripts.

topics.title: The Translation of the Bible
topics.explanation: The Bible has been given to the world in translation, beginning with the Septuagint, the Greek version made in Alexandria, and the Vulgate, Jerome's Latin translation that served the Western Church for a millennium. The Reformation produced vernacular versions — Luther's German, Tyndale's English — that were revolutions in language and in faith. Modern translation theory distinguishes formal (literal) from dynamic (thought-for-thought) equivalence, and the best versions aim at faithfulness to the original meaning in idiomatic modern speech. The history of translation is the history of the Word going forth to the nations.
concepts: The Septuagint and the Vulgate as landmark versions
The Reformation vernacular translations
Formal versus dynamic equivalence
Translation as the going forth of the Word
topics.context: Luther translated by the principle of 'the mother in her house'; Tyndale's New Testament (1526) shaped the English Bible.
topics.takeaway: The Bible was meant to be read by all God's people in their own tongues; faithful translation is a ministry of the Word.

topics.title: The Biblical Doctrine of Revelation
topics.explanation: Revelation is God's self-communication to his creatures, making known what could not otherwise be known. The Bible presents a general revelation in creation and conscience, which shows that God exists and is powerful (Ps 19; Rom 1:20), and a special, saving revelation in the history of the covenant and, supremely, in the person and work of Jesus Christ (Heb 1:1-2). Special revelation is not a further disclosure of moral truth but the communication of the triune God himself for the purpose of salvation. The Word that is revealed becomes the Word that is written — Scripture is revelation committed to memory.
concepts: Revelation as God's self-communication
General and special revelation distinguished and related
Christ as the summit of revelation
Revelation committed to memory in Scripture
topics.context: The doctrine was shaped against natural philosophy and the Gnostic claim to a secret, superior revelation.
topics.takeaway: Revelation is God making himself known for salvation; Scripture is that revelation preserved in writing for all generations.

topics.title: General and Special Revelation
topics.explanation: General revelation is God's self-disclosure to all people in and through creation, providence and conscience; it is universal, sufficient to render all without excuse (Rom 1:19-20), but not sufficient for salvation. Special revelation is God's self-communication within the covenant, in the theophanies, the prophets, the Word made flesh, and finally in Scripture; it is particular, saving, and progressively culminating in Christ. The two are not rivals: general revelation prepares the mind and conscience, while special revelation brings the saving knowledge of God. Both point to the one true God, but only the special reveals him as Father, Son and Spirit.
concepts: General revelation: universal, condemnatory, insufficient for salvation
Special revelation: particular, saving, culminating in Christ
The relation of the two: preparation and fulfilment
The triune self-communication as the goal of all revelation
topics.context: The distinction was sharpened in the Reformation and in the debates over natural theology.
topics.takeaway: All people see God's glory in creation; only the special revelation in Christ makes known God as Saviour.

topics.title: The Interpretation of Scripture: Principles of Hermeneutics
topics.explanation: Hermeneutics is the science of interpretation. The fundamental principle is that Scripture must be interpreted according to its plain, grammatical-historical sense: what the text meant to its original authors and readers, in its literary and historical context. The higher principle is that Scripture interprets Scripture (analogia fidei) — no passage may be taken as the standard of faith if it conflicts with the whole tenor of the Bible. The reader brings to the text the same spirit that produced it: faith, humility, and the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Grammar, history, literary form and context are the ordinary tools of the task.
concepts: The grammatical-historical sense as the starting point
Analogia fidei — Scripture interprets Scripture
Literary form and the rules of each genre
The role of the Spirit in the interpretation of the Word
topics.context: The Reformed tradition developed the fourfold sense (literal, allegorical, moral, anagogical) into the primacy of the literal sense.
topics.takeaway: The Bible is to be read as it was written: in its grammar, its history, its context, and under the rule of the whole of Scripture.

topics.title: The Literary Forms and Context of the Bible
topics.explanation: The Bible is not a single book but a library of literary forms: narrative, law, poetry, prophecy, apocalyptic, wisdom, gospel, epistle and apocalypse. Each form has its own conventions, and the responsible interpreter must read each text as the kind of literature it is. Reading a psalm as a scientific report, or a parable as history, produces absurdities. The historical and literary context — the author, the original audience, the situation, the purpose — is the first question the interpreter must answer. Only by respecting the literary forms can the theological meaning of each text be recovered and applied.
concepts: The major biblical genres and their conventions
Context: author, audience, situation, purpose
The danger of reading the wrong genre as the wrong form
From interpretation to application
topics.context: The rise of literary criticism in the twentieth century enriched, though sometimes distorted, biblical interpretation.
topics.takeaway: To interpret the Bible well, one must first understand the kind of book one is reading — and the world in which it was written.

topics.title: The Bible as the Rule of Christian Doctrine
topics.explanation: Because the Bible is the Word of God, it is the final rule (norma normans) of all Christian doctrine, worship and life. No creed, no church decision, no private experience may override or stand above the plain teaching of Scripture. This is the principle of sola Scriptura in its full force: the Scriptures are sufficient for everything necessary for faith and life, and they alone are the final court of appeal. The Church's creeds and confessions are valuable, but they are norma normata — norms that are themselves normed by Scripture. The student of theology who holds this principle has a secure foundation for the whole of the course.
concepts: Scripture as norma normans, the final court of appeal
The sufficiency of Scripture for faith and life
Creeds as norma normata — subordinate to Scripture
The practical consequences for doctrine and conscience
topics.context: Sola Scriptura was the formal principle of the Reformation, recovered from the Church's own practice of appealing to Scripture.
topics.takeaway: The Bible is the supreme and final rule of doctrine; all other witnesses are valued insofar as they agree with it.

ideas: Both Testaments are covenant libraries, recognised by the faithful community as the Word of God.
The canon is closed: the apostolic witness is complete, and the Church guards what God has already spoken.
Inspiration and authority rest on God as Author; the text is inerrant in the originals and securely transmitted.
Interpretation follows the grammatical-historical sense, governed by the whole of Scripture (analogia fidei).
summary.connections: The questions of inspiration and authority answered here become the ground of the doctrine of revelation in the systematic modules; the method of interpretation is used in every biblical and doctrinal study that follows.
summary.progression: With the formation, authority and interpretation of the Bible established, the programme ascends to the supreme subject of theology: the one true God.

modules.title: Theology Proper: The Doctrine of God
modules.divider_intro: The being, attributes and triune life of the one true God — the centre of the whole theological edifice.

intro.discipline: Theology proper is the doctrine of God: his existence, his attributes, his works, and the mystery of the trinity of persons in the unity of the Godhead. It is 'proper' in the technical sense that it treats God in himself, before treating his relation to the world.
intro.context: The doctrine of God is the root and crown of the Christian faith. The creeds begin with God the Father, and the entire confession moves outward from the divine being to creation, redemption and glory. Whatever the Church says about Christ, the Spirit and salvation is controlled by what it says about God.
intro.relevance: Theology proper is the doctrinal centre of the programme: the attributes explained here become the grammar by which every later doctrine — incarnation, atonement, resurrection — is interpreted.
intro.focus: To articulate the existence, attributes, sovereignty and triune personhood of God as Scripture and the creeds confess them.

topics.title: The Existence and Self-Revelation of God
topics.explanation: Christian theology confesses that the God of Israel exists, is one, and has spoken. The classical arguments — cosmological, teleological, moral — are offered by the Church as rational aids to belief, but the Christian conviction rests primarily on God's self-revelation: in creation, in the history of Israel, and supremely in Jesus Christ. The divine names of the Old Testament — YHWH, El Shaddai, El Elyon — are not abstract titles but the language of a God who makes himself known and is known. The first words of the Decalogue presuppose the existence of the one true God.
concepts: Revelation as God's self-disclosure, not bare information
The classical arguments as aids to belief
The divine names: YHWH ('I AM'), El Shaddai, El Elyon
The knowledge of God as the first article of faith
topics.context: From Anselm to Plantinga, the status of the classical arguments has been debated; the historic position subordinates them to revelation.
topics.takeaway: The God of Christian theology is not a hypothesis but a self-disclosing Person — known, named and approachable.

topics.title: The Incommunicable Attributes of God
topics.explanation: The incommunicable attributes distinguish God absolutely from all creatures. Aseity: God is self-existent, depending on nothing but his own nature (Ex 3:14). Eternity: God is without beginning or end (Ps 90:2). Immutability: God is not subject to change in his being, perfections or purposes (Mal 3:6). Omnipresence: God is present everywhere in his power, knowledge and care (Ps 139:7-12). These are not limitations upon the infinite God but the perfection of his freedom: he needs nothing, is independent of all, and is everywhere at home.
concepts: Aseity — self-existence (actus purus in the scholastic language)
Eternity — timelessness or endless duration, the major interpretations
Immutability — constancy of character, not emotional inactivity
Omnipresence — ubiquity of presence in creation and beyond
topics.context: Aquinas's doctrine of pure act and the Reformed emphasis on divine simplicity both guard God's transcendence.
topics.takeaway: The incommunicable attributes answer 'What is God like?' — a God who needs nothing, changes in nothing and is everywhere present.

topics.title: The Communicable Attributes of God
topics.explanation: The communicable attributes are those in which creatures bear a finite likeness to God. Omniscience: God knows all things, actual and possible (Ps 139:4). Omnipotence: God can do all that is consistent with his nature and purpose (Gen 18:14). Holiness: God is other than, and morally perfect above, all creatures (Isa 6:3). Love: God is love in the fullest biblical sense — self-giving, covenantal, the ground of redemption (1 John 4:8). Faithfulness, justice and truth complete the set, showing that God's character is not merely powerful but personally trustworthy.
concepts: Omniscience — including the range of divine foreknowledge
Omnipotence — power consistent with God's holy nature
Holiness — moral perfection and transcendent otherness (qadosh)
Love — agape as the self-giving ground of covenant and redemption
topics.context: The image of God (imago Dei) is the creaturely reflection of these attributes — the foundation of the doctrine of man.
topics.takeaway: In the communicable attributes creation bears, in limited form, the signature of its Creator.

topics.title: The Sovereignty and Divine Decree of God
topics.explanation: The sovereignty of God means that he is the supreme ruler over all things, and that nothing happens except by his will or permission. The doctrine of the decree holds that God, from eternity, has ordained whatever comes to pass, not by blind fate but by the free, wise and holy counsel of his own will (Eph 1:11; Acts 4:27-28). The decree is the ground of God's providence over all events, including the fall and the redemption it made necessary. The doctrine safeguards the unity of history under God while he remains the only Author of sin.
concepts: Sovereignty: God as supreme ruler over all events
The decree: ordination of all that comes to pass
The decree and the permission of sin
The unity and purpose of history under God
topics.context: The decree was the centre of the Reformed confessions (Westminster, Canons of Dort) and of the Arminian controversy.
topics.takeaway: All history unfolds under the wise, holy and free decree of the sovereign God.

topics.title: The Omniscience of God
topics.explanation: God's omniscience means that he knows all things: the past, the present and the future; all facts, all possibilities, and the inward thoughts of the heart (Ps 139:1-4). The doctrine raises the classic questions of the extent of divine foreknowledge, the relation of foreknowledge to human freedom, and the so-called 'middle knowledge' of some scholastics. The biblical witness is plain that nothing is hidden from the Lord's eye, and that his knowledge of the future is certain. Christian doctrine affirms that God's foreknowledge does not destroy human responsibility but is exercised within his sovereign decree.
concepts: Omniscience: all actual and possible things
Divine foreknowledge and its certainty
The relation of foreknowledge to human freedom
The scholastic doctrine of middle knowledge (scientia media)
topics.context: Molinism (Luis de Molina, 1580) sought to reconcile foreknowledge and freedom via middle knowledge.
topics.takeaway: God knows all things certainly; his foreknowledge is the foundation of his sure guidance of all events.

topics.title: The Omnipotence of God
topics.explanation: God's omnipotence means that he is able to do all that he wills, and all that is consistent with his nature. The omnipotence of God is not the power to do what is logically absurd or what is contrary to his own holy character (he cannot lie, Acts 1:9; he cannot sin, Jam 1:13). Rather, it is the power to accomplish everything his wise and good purposes require. The Scripture sets the bounds: 'Is anything too hard for the Lord?' (Gen 18:14). Creation, preservation, redemption and the final consummation are the great displays of a power that is infinite, unhindered, and exercised in freedom and wisdom.
concepts: Omnipotence as power consistent with God's nature
The impossibility of logical absurdity and moral evil in God
Creation, preservation and redemption as displays of power
The freedom and wisdom that qualify the exercise of power
topics.context: The 'omnipotence paradox' (can God make a stone he cannot lift?) is a linguistic confusion, not a real limit on God.
topics.takeaway: God is able to do all that his holy, wise purposes require; his power is infinite and unhindered.

topics.title: The Omnipresence of God
topics.explanation: God's omnipresence means that he is present in all places at all times. This is not a pantheistic diffusion of God into nature, but the presence of the personal God everywhere by his knowledge, power and care (Ps 139:7-12; Jer 23:23-24). The doctrine has three aspects: God's essence fills all things, his knowledge observes all things, and his power acts upon all things. Yet Scripture also speaks of God's special, indwelling presence with his people — in the tabernacle, in the temple, and in the believer by the Spirit — which is a presence of favour distinct from mere ubiquity.
concepts: Omnipresence: essence, knowledge and power in all places
The distinction from pantheistic immanence
The special presence of God with his covenant people
The presence of the Spirit in the believer
topics.context: The debate over the relation of God's presence to the material world shaped the doctrines of transubstantiation and of the Lord's Supper.
topics.takeaway: God is everywhere by his presence, yet specially present to his people in grace.

topics.title: The Eternity and Immutability of God
topics.explanation: God's eternity means that he exists without beginning, end or succession; he is 'the Amen, the faithful and true Witness' (Rev 21:5) and his is 'the life that was with the Father' (John 1:2). Whether eternity is best understood as timelessness (the Boethian 'whole and perfect possession of endless life') or as endless duration is a live question, but both affirm that God is not subject to time as creatures are. God's immutability means that he does not change in his being, perfections, purposes or promises (Mal 3:6; Num 23:19). This does not make him a frozen abstraction; the unchangeable God acts, responds and loves with perfect constancy.
concepts: Eternity: without beginning, end or succession
The Boethian definition: whole and perfect possession of life
Immutability: constancy in being, perfections and purposes
The relation of immutability to divine action and response
topics.context: Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy gave the classic definition of eternity; Aquinas developed it in the Summa.
topics.takeaway: The eternal, immutable God is the sure foundation of every promise and the unshakable ground of the believer's hope.

topics.title: The Holiness of God
topics.explanation: Holiness (qadosh) is the attribute that sets God above all else and marks him as wholly other. It has two aspects: in itself, God's separation from all creatures and from all sin; and in relation, his transcendent purity and moral perfection. The seraphim cry 'Holy, holy, holy' (Isa 6:3), and Isaiah's encounter with the holy God is the root of his own sense of sin. Holiness is the ground of the moral law and the standard of all ethics: 'Be holy, for I am holy' (1 Pet 1:16). It is also the attribute that most clearly distinguishes the triune God from the many gods of the world.
concepts: Qadosh: separateness and moral purity
The twofold aspect: in itself and in relation
Holiness as the ground of the moral law
The call to holiness in the people of God
topics.context: The holiness movement of the nineteenth century and the modern emphasis on holiness in evangelism trace directly to this attribute.
topics.takeaway: God's holiness sets him above all, is the standard of all morality, and is the ground of the call to be holy.

topics.title: The Love and Goodness of God
topics.explanation: God is love (1 John 4:8) — not merely loving, but love itself in the fullest biblical sense. His love is self-giving (agape), the ground of the covenant, the motive of creation and the cause of redemption. It is demonstrated in the sending of the Son (John 3:16) and in the gift of the Spirit. God's goodness is his love expressed in all his dealings: he is good to all, the source of every good gift (Jam 1:17), and his goodness is the ground of both the natural order and the moral life. The two attributes are the positive side of the same reality: a God who is personal, near, and for his creatures.
concepts: Agape: self-giving, covenantal love
Love as the ground of creation and redemption
Goodness: the source of every good gift
The demonstration of love in the sending of the Son
topics.context: The Johannine 'God is love' and the Pauline 'love of God in Christ' are the scriptural anchors of the doctrine.
topics.takeaway: God is love itself; his self-giving love is the motive of all his works and the ground of all blessing.

topics.title: The Justice, Truth and Faithfulness of God
topics.explanation: God's justice means that he is perfectly right in all his dealings, rewarding good and punishing evil with exacting fairness. His truth means that he is the standard of all reality and that his word is reliable — 'God is not a man, that he should lie' (Num 23:19). His faithfulness means that he keeps his covenant promises and remains constant to his people across the generations (Lam 3:22-23; 1 Cor 1:9). These three attributes together guarantee that the moral order is secure, that Scripture can be trusted, and that the believer's hope is certain. They are the attributes on which the law, the gospel and the eschatological hope all depend.
concepts: Justice: perfect rightness in all dealings
Truth: God as the standard of reality and of his word
Faithfulness: constancy to the covenant promises
The three together as the ground of law, gospel and hope
topics.context: The Reformed confessions stress divine faithfulness as the ground of the assurance of the covenant.
topics.takeaway: God's justice, truth and faithfulness make the moral order secure and the believer's hope certain.

topics.title: The Doctrine of the Trinity
topics.explanation: The doctrine of the Trinity confesses that there is one God in three co-equal, co-eternal persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The unity of the Godhead is absolute — there is one divine essence, not three gods — and the distinction of the persons is real, not merely modal. The persons are distinct in their relations of origin (the Father begets the Son, the Spirit proceeds) but equal in essence, power and glory. The doctrine is not a speculative addition but the Church's confession of what Scripture reveals: the one God who acts as Father, Son and Spirit. It is the great mystery of the Christian faith, guarded by the creeds.
concepts: One essence (ousia), three persons (hypostases)
The relations of origin: begotten and proceeding
The distinction from modalism, sabellianism and tritheism
The Trinity as the confession of the one acting God
topics.context: The doctrine was defined at Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381) against Arianism and other heresies.
topics.takeaway: The Trinity is the one God — Father, Son and Spirit — confessed as the ground of all Christian doctrine and worship.

topics.title: The Biblical Basis of the Doctrine of the Trinity
topics.explanation: The doctrine of the Trinity is not found in a single proof-text but is the necessary interpretation of the whole of Scripture. The Old Testament affirms the one God while speaking in ways that anticipate the persons (the plural 'let us make,' Gen 1:26; the Angel of the LORD; the Spirit as a distinct agent). The New Testament is explicit: the Father sends the Son, the Son is worshipped as God, the Spirit is called Lord and God, and the three are named together in the baptismal formula and the benedictions. The Church's task was not to invent the Trinity but to give doctrinal form to what the apostles confessed. The doctrine is thus biblical, not merely creational.
concepts: The Old Testament one-God with anticipations of the persons
The New Testament explicitness: Father, Son, Spirit named together
The divine titles of the Son and the Spirit
The creed as the confession of what Scripture reveals
topics.context: The Trinitarian formula of the Great Commission and the Johannine prologue are the classic New Testament anchors.
topics.takeaway: The Trinity is the doctrine forced upon the Church by the totality of Scripture's witness to the one God in three persons.

topics.title: God the Father: The First Person of the Trinity
topics.explanation: The Father is the first person of the Trinity, the unbegotten source from whom the Son is eternally begotten and the Spirit proceeds. He is 'Father' not in the sense of a mere originator but as the personal, loving source of all — the Father of Jesus Christ and, in Christ, of all believers. The Old Testament presents him as Creator, Covenant-God, Judge and King; the New Testament reveals him as the Father who gives the Son and the Spirit to those who believe. To know the Father is the goal of all theology and the privilege of the child of God (John 14:7-9; Eph 1:3-6).
concepts: The Father as unbegotten source of the Godhead
Father as personal, loving source, not mere originator
The Father as Creator, Covenant-God, Judge and King
Knowing the Father as the goal of theology and the privilege of the child
topics.context: The Father is named first in the baptismal formula and in the benedictions, reflecting the order of the persons.
topics.takeaway: The Father is the source and goal of all: the one who gives the Son and the Spirit and to whom all things are reconciled.

ideas: God exists, is one, and has spoken — the starting point of all doctrine.
The incommunicable attributes define God's transcendence; the communicable attributes his similarity to creation.
God is sovereign, holy, loving, just and true — the ground of law, gospel and hope.
The one God is confessed as three co-equal persons: Father, Son and Spirit.
summary.connections: The attributes explained here are the grammar of every later module: the incarnation is read by them, salvation is measured by them, and the Church's worship confesses them. The Trinity is the root from which the doctrines of Christ and of the Spirit grow.
summary.progression: Having seen the one God in himself, the programme descends to his works in the world: creation, providence and the angelic order.

modules.title: Creation, Providence and Angels
modules.divider_intro: God's work in making, sustaining and ruling the world, and the unseen order of angels and spirits.

intro.discipline: This module treats God's relation to the world he has made: the doctrine of creation, its good purpose, the doctrine of providence by which God rules all events, the problem of evil, and the doctrine of the unseen order — angels, Satan and the evil spirits.
intro.context: Creation theology is the answer to every worldview that reduces the world to matter, chance or self-cause. From Genesis through the Psalms and the New Testament creation and providence are the framework within which redemption is understood: the world is God's, and its history is his story.
intro.relevance: The doctrine of creation grounds the dignity of the natural order and of the human being; the doctrine of providence grounds the Christian's confidence in suffering and in history; the angelic doctrine completes the picture of God's world as a whole.
intro.focus: To understand creation as God's good work, providence as his ruling hand, and the angelic order as part of the created world under God's sovereignty.

topics.title: The Doctrine of Creation
topics.explanation: The doctrine of creation confesses that the one true God, by the word of his power, brought the whole universe into being, and that the world derives everything it has — existence, being and good — from him. Creation is both creatio ex nihilo (out of nothing, without pre-existing matter) and creatio continua (the continuous preservation of what has been made). The world is not self-existent, nor is it an emanation of the divine essence, but a free act of God's will and love. The doctrine stands against atheism, pantheism, deism and every form of dualism that places a power beside or above the Creator.
concepts: Creatio ex nihilo — creation out of nothing
Creatio continua — the continuous preservation of creation
The world as a free act of God's will and love
The doctrine against atheism, pantheism and dualism
topics.context: The doctrine was defined against Gnostic and Manichaean dualisms in the early Church and reaffirmed at the early councils.
topics.takeaway: The world is God's free creation, sustained by his power; it owes its whole being to the Creator.

topics.title: The Days and Modes of Creation
topics.explanation: Genesis 1 presents the work of creation in six days, with a seventh day of rest. The 'days' have been understood in several responsible ways: as literal twenty-four-hour days (day-age and framework views offer alternative readings), or as a literary structure that reveals the order and purpose of creation. The modes of creation include the formation of the heavens and earth, the separation and filling of the world, and the crowning work of the creation of man. Whatever the interpretation of the days, the text's primary purpose is theological: to show that the one God, by his word, made an orderly, good world in which man holds a place of honour.
concepts: The six-day structure and its literary framework
Literal, day-age and framework interpretations
The order: formation and filling of the world
The theological purpose of the creation account
topics.context: The days of Genesis 1 have been debated from the early Church (Augustine) to the modern debate over evolution.
topics.takeaway: The creation account's chief aim is theological: to reveal the one God who made an orderly, good world and crowned it with man.

topics.title: Creation, Evolution and the Interpretation of Genesis
topics.explanation: The relation of the doctrine of creation to the scientific theory of evolution is one of the great questions of modern theology. The responsible Christian position affirms that God is the Creator of all things and that the details of the creative process are not fully revealed. Some Christians accept an old-earth or evolutionary account of the development of nature as the means God used; others hold to a younger earth and a more literal reading of the days. What all confessing Christians affirm is that the soul of man is the direct work of God, and that the world, whatever its developmental history, is God's good creation under his providence.
concepts: God as Creator: the non-negotiable confession
The open question of the creative process and time
Old-earth, young-earth and evolutionary positions
The special creation of the human soul
topics.context: The debate intensified after Darwin (1859); the Young Earth Creationist and Old Earth Evangelical responses remain in tension.
topics.takeaway: All Christians confess God as Creator; they differ on the means and timing, but agree that man's soul is God's special work.

topics.title: The Goodness and Purpose of Creation
topics.explanation: The creation account is marked by repeated affirmations that creation is good — 'it was good,' and finally 'it was very good' (Gen 1:31). The world is not a prison, a mistake, or an illusion, but the good work of a good God. Creation has a purpose: it is made for the glory of God and for the dwelling of man, who is set over it in stewardship. The goodness of creation is the ground of the Christian's responsible care for the natural world and of the joy with which the believer receives God's gifts. The doctrine stands against every asceticism that despises the body and every materialism that worships the creature.
concepts: Creation as 'very good' — the repeated affirmation
The world made for God's glory and man's stewardship
The ground of responsible care for the natural world
The balance against asceticism and materialism
topics.context: The doctrine of creation's goodness underlies the modern environmental ethics and the theology of stewardship.
topics.takeaway: Creation is good, purposeful, and entrusted to man; the believer receives it with joy and stewards it with responsibility.

topics.title: The Doctrine of Divine Providence
topics.explanation: Providence is the doctrine that God, after creating the world, continuously preserves it, governs it, and directs all things to the end he has purposed (Eph 1:11; Ps 103:19). It is the 'government of God' — not a distant first cause but a present, personal ruler. Providence extends to all events, from the falling of a sparrow to the rise and fall of nations. It is the ground of the Christian's confidence that history is not random but is under God's rule, and that in the end his purposes will be accomplished. The doctrine is the continuing aspect of creation: God does not merely make the world but keeps it in being and orders it to his good end.
concepts: Preservation: God keeps the world in being
Government: God directs all events to his purpose
The extent of providence over all events
Providence as the ground of confidence in history
topics.context: The Reformed confessions give the most developed statements of providence, distinguishing God's permitting from his ordering.
topics.takeaway: God does not merely create but continually preserves and governs the world, ordering all things to his good purpose.

topics.title: Providence, Prayer and Human Responsibility
topics.explanation: The doctrine of providence raises the question of the relation of God's rule to human action and prayer. Providence does not abolish human responsibility; rather, God works through the free actions of his creatures. Prayer is not a means of informing or changing God but a means by which God ordains to accomplish what he has purposed. The Reformed doctrine holds that God ordains both the end and the means, and that prayer is one of the means he has appointed. Human responsibility is real — men are the authors of their own acts — yet all events, including human acts, are under God's sovereign governance. The two are held together without either being absorbed into the other.
concepts: God works through the free actions of creatures
Prayer as an ordained means, not a change in God
Human responsibility as real authorship of acts
The holding together of sovereignty and responsibility
topics.context: The debate over secondary causes and divine concurrence runs from the medieval philosophers to the Reformed confessions.
topics.takeaway: God rules all events, yet works through the free, responsible actions of his creatures, prayer among them.

topics.title: The Problem of Evil and Suffering
topics.explanation: The problem of evil asks how a good, almighty God can permit evil and suffering. The Christian answer has several parts. Evil entered the world through the free revolt of the angels and of man, not from God, who is the only Author of sin. God permits evil to serve his wise and holy purposes, and he limits it, redeems it, and will finally overcome it in the work of Christ. The suffering of the righteous is not a sign of God's absence but the means by which he sanctifies his people and displays the glory of the cross. The answer is ultimately eschatological: evil is real and serious, but it is not the last word, for God will make all things new.
concepts: The origin of evil in the free revolt of creatures
God as not the author of sin but its governor
The redemptive purpose in suffering
The eschatological defeat of evil in Christ
topics.context: The book of Job and the theodicies of Augustine, Leibniz and the Reformed fathers form the classic treatments.
topics.takeaway: Evil is real but not ultimate; God permits it to serve his holy purposes and will finally overthrow it in Christ.

topics.title: The Doctrine of the Angelic World
topics.explanation: The Bible teaches that God has created an order of spiritual, intelligent beings — the angels — who serve him and minister to his people. They are personal, incorporeal beings, superior to men in power and knowledge but still creatures, made by God and subject to him. The Scripture speaks of the heavenly host, of the angels who worshipped at the giving of the law, and of the many thousands of angels who attend the throne. The doctrine of the angelic world completes the picture of God's creation as including both the visible and the invisible order, all under the sovereignty of the Creator.
concepts: Angels as personal, incorporeal creatures
Their superiority to men in power and knowledge
The heavenly host and the worship of the angels
The angelic order as part of creation under God
topics.context: The doctrine of the angels was defined against the Gnostic and Manichaean exaltation of the spiritual powers.
topics.takeaway: The angels are God's spiritual creatures, superior to men yet subject to him, who serve him and minister to his people.

topics.title: The Nature and Order of the Angels
topics.explanation: The tradition of the Church, drawing on the Scripture and on the ancient classifications, has spoken of a hierarchy or order of the angels — the seraphim, cherubim, thrones, dominions, virtues, powers, principalities, archangels and angels. The Scripture names the seraphim and cherubim of Isaiah and Ezekiel, and speaks of principalities and powers (Eph 1:21; Col 2:15). The exact structure of the hierarchy is not a matter of dogma, and the responsible theologian treats the nine-order scheme as a useful summary rather than a precise doctrine. What is certain is that the angels are numerous, powerful, and arranged in an order under God, all performing their assigned ministries.
concepts: The named angels: seraphim, cherubim, archangels
The principalities and powers of the epistles
The nine-order scheme as summary, not dogma
The number and power of the heavenly host
topics.context: Pseudo-Dionysius's Celestial Hierarchy (c. 500) is the classic source of the nine-order classification.
topics.takeaway: The angels are numerous and powerful, arranged in an order under God, each performing his assigned ministry.

topics.title: The Fall of Satan and the Devil
topics.explanation: The Bible teaches that Satan, originally a created angel of high rank, rebelled against God and became the chief of the evil spirits. His fall was a free revolt, rooted in pride — 'I will be exalted above the heads of the other stars of God, I will sit upon the mountain of the congregation, I will be like the Most High' (Isa 14:13-14). From that time he has been the adversary of God and his people, the tempter of man and the author of evil in the world. He is a real personal being, not a mere symbol, yet he is a creature, finite and under God's sovereignty, whose power is limited and whose end is certain.
concepts: Satan as a created angel who rebelled in pride
His fall as a free, moral revolt
His role as adversary, tempter and author of evil
His finitude and ultimate defeat under God's sovereignty
topics.context: The identification of the 'Lucifer' of Isaiah 14 with Satan is the traditional, though debated, interpretation.
topics.takeaway: Satan is a real, fallen angel, the chief of evil spirits, who is finite, under God's sovereignty, and certain to be defeated.

topics.title: The Activity of Evil Spirits
topics.explanation: The Scripture teaches that the evil spirits, under Satan, are active in the world, tempting men, oppressing the ungodly, and seeking to hinder the work of God. Yet their power is limited: they are subject to God's sovereignty, and their ultimate end is the lake of fire. The believer is not without defence: the armour of God, the authority of the name of Christ, and the power of the Spirit guard him against the wiles of the devil. The doctrine is to be held in balance — the reality of evil spirits is not to be denied, nor is it to be exaggerated into a kind of demonic dualism. The Christian lives under the sovereignty of God, in whom all powers are finally subject.
concepts: The activity of evil spirits: temptation, oppression, hindrance
Their limited power under God's sovereignty
The believer's defence: armour, name, and Spirit
The balance against denial and against demonic dualism
topics.context: The doctrine of evil spirits is to be held against both rationalist denial and an excessive demonological emphasis.
topics.takeaway: The evil spirits are real but limited; the believer is guarded by God and certain of the final victory in Christ.

topics.title: Creation in Relation to the Doctrine of God
topics.explanation: The doctrine of creation brings the doctrine of God to bear upon the world. Creation is the first great work of God, and it reveals his attributes — his power, wisdom, goodness and providential care. The world is the theatre in which God displays his glory and accomplishes his purposes. The doctrine of creation thus grounds the Christian's view of the natural world, of history, and of his own place in it: man is the crown of creation, made in the image of God and set to steward his world. Creation is the context within which the redemptive work of Christ is understood — the reconciliation of all things to God (Col 1:20).
concepts: Creation as the first work revealing God's attributes
The world as the theatre of God's glory
Man as the crown of creation and steward
Creation as the context of redemption
topics.context: The doctrine of creation is the bridge from theology proper to the doctrines of man and of redemption.
topics.takeaway: Creation is God's first work, revealing his glory and setting the stage for the redemption accomplished in Christ.

ideas: God created the world freely out of nothing and continues to preserve it.
Creation is good, purposeful, and entrusted to man as steward.
God governs all events by his providence, working through the free, responsible actions of creatures.
The angelic order, including the fallen Satan, is part of creation under God's sovereignty.
summary.connections: Creation and providence are the context for the doctrines of man and of redemption; the goodness of creation grounds the dignity of the human being, and providence grounds the Christian's confidence in history and in suffering.
summary.progression: Having seen God's work in creation and providence, the programme turns to the crown of creation: the doctrine of man, his image, his fall and his estate.

modules.title: The Doctrine of Man
modules.divider_intro: The image of God, the constitution of the human being, the fall, and the estate of sin in which mankind now stands.

intro.discipline: The doctrine of man (theological anthropology) treats the nature, origin, constitution, and estate of the human being: his creation in the image of God, his fall into sin, and the condition of the race as a result. It answers the question, 'What is man?' from the standpoint of revelation.
intro.context: Anthropology is the pivot between the doctrine of creation and the doctrine of salvation. The dignity of man rests on the image of God; his misery rests on the fall; and both together explain why redemption was needed and why it was given.
intro.relevance: The doctrine of man is the ground of the Christian view of the person, of human dignity, of moral responsibility, and of the need for grace. Every ethic, psychology and social theory ultimately stands or falls on its anthropology.
intro.focus: To understand man as God made him, as he fell, and as he now is — and so to see the need for the redemption that the later modules will unfold.

topics.title: The Biblical Doctrine of Man
topics.explanation: The biblical doctrine of man begins with the confession that man is the creature of the one true God, made by his direct act and not by a process of nature. Genesis presents the creation of man as distinct from that of the animals: 'Then the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living being' (Gen 2:7). Man is at once a physical being, made of the dust, and a spiritual being, given the breath of God. The Scripture presents man as a unity of body and soul, made in the image of God, set over the world in stewardship, and brought into a covenant relation with his Creator.
concepts: Man as the direct creature of God, distinct from the animals
The twofold origin: dust of the ground and breath of God
Man as the unity of body and soul
Man made in the image of God and set as steward
topics.context: The doctrine of man was defined against the Gnostic devaluation of the body and the Platonic devaluation of matter.
topics.takeaway: Man is God's special creation, a unity of body and soul, made in his image and set to steward his world.

topics.title: The Image of God in Man
topics.explanation: The image of God (imago Dei) is the distinguishing mark of man among the creatures, and the ground of his dignity. It has been understood in several complementary ways. Substantively, it refers to those attributes in which man resembles God — knowledge, righteousness and holiness (Eph 4:24). Relationally, it refers to man's being made for communion with God and for rule over the world. Functionally, it refers to man's vocation as God's representative and steward on the earth. The image is not a quality that can be fully recovered by human effort; it was marred by the fall and is being restored by the work of Christ (Col 3:10; 2 Cor 3:18).
concepts: Substantive: knowledge, righteousness and holiness
Relational: made for communion with God and rule
Functional: man as God's representative and steward
The image marred by the fall and restored by Christ
topics.context: The imago Dei is the scriptural foundation of the doctrine of human dignity and of the sanctity of human life.
topics.takeaway: The image of God is the ground of man's dignity; it was marred by the fall and is being renewed by the work of Christ.

topics.title: The Nature and Composition of Man
topics.explanation: The Scripture presents man as a unity of body and soul, not as two separate substances joined together. The terms used — body, soul, spirit, heart, mind — describe the one person from different aspects. The traditional views are trichotomism (body, soul, spirit) and dichotomism (body and soul, with 'soul' and 'spirit' used interchangeably for the inner man). The responsible position is that man is one person, physically constituted by the body and spiritually constituted by the soul or spirit, the two being inseparably united in this life and separated only at death. The doctrine guards against both the materialism that reduces man to body and the idealism that reduces him to spirit.
concepts: Man as one person, not two substances
The terms: body, soul, spirit, heart, mind
Trichotomism and dichotomism
The inseparable union of body and soul in this life
topics.context: The debate over trichotomism and dichotomism has run through the Church from the early fathers to modern psychology.
topics.takeaway: Man is one person, a unity of body and soul, the two being inseparably joined in this life.

topics.title: Man in the Garden of Eden
topics.explanation: The Garden of Eden presents man in his original, unfallen estate. Adam was created in the image of God, placed in a perfect environment, and given a vocation and a command. He was set to work the garden and to keep it (Gen 2:15), and he was given the command not to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen 2:16-17). Adam and Eve were in a state of innocence, in communion with God, and in harmony with one another and with the world. The Eden narrative establishes the original righteousness of man, the reality of the moral law, and the possibility of a genuine fall — for the command presupposes the freedom to obey or to disobey.
concepts: Man created in innocence and in communion with God
The vocation to work the garden and keep it
The command and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil
The original righteousness and the possibility of the fall
topics.context: The Eden narrative is the framework for the doctrine of the covenant of works and of original righteousness.
topics.takeaway: Adam was created in innocence, in communion with God, and given a vocation and a command that made the fall possible.

topics.title: The Covenant of Works
topics.explanation: The covenant of works is the name given to the arrangement under which Adam stood in the Garden of Eden. God made a covenant with man, promising life upon obedience and threatening death upon disobedience. Adam was the federal head of the race, and his obedience or disobedience would have affected all his descendants. The covenant of works is not explicitly named in the Scripture but is inferred from the Eden narrative and from the Pauline doctrine of Adam as the head of the old order (Rom 5:12-21; 1 Cor 15:21-22). It establishes the principle of federal headship and explains how the fall of one man could bring sin and death to all.
concepts: The covenant of works: life for obedience, death for disobedience
Adam as federal head of the race
The inference from the Eden narrative and Paul's doctrine of Adam
The principle of federal headship
topics.context: The doctrine of the covenant of works was developed in the Reformed scholastics and is a key to the Pauline doctrine of Adam.
topics.takeaway: The covenant of works established Adam as federal head, so that his fall brought sin and death to all his descendants.

topics.title: The Fall of Man
topics.explanation: The fall of man is the event in which Adam and Eve, under the temptation of the serpent, disobeyed God's command and ate of the forbidden fruit. The serpent's strategy was to cast doubt on God's word and to exalt self — 'You will not surely die' and 'you will be like God' (Gen 3:4-5). Adam and Eve chose to trust themselves rather than God, and in doing so they sinned, were cast out of the garden, and brought upon themselves and their posterity the penalties of the curse. The fall is the origin of the sinful condition of the race, and it is the event that explains the universal reign of sin and death. It is the turning point of human history.
concepts: The temptation and the strategy of the serpent
The choice to trust self rather than God
The penalties of the curse upon Adam, Eve and their posterity
The fall as the origin of the sinful condition of the race
topics.context: The fall is the event that explains the universal reign of sin and death and the need for redemption.
topics.takeaway: The fall was the choice to trust self rather than God; it brought sin and death upon the whole race and explains the need for redemption.

topics.title: The Nature of Sin
topics.explanation: Sin is the transgression of the law of God (1 John 3:4) — every act, thought or disposition that falls short of or violates the holy will of God. Sin has an object, which is God, and its essence is a turning of the will from God to self. It is at once a personal act and a state of alienation from God. The Scripture describes sin in many ways: as missing the mark (hamartia), as iniquity or crookedness (avedia), as lawlessness (anomia), and as unbelief. Sin is not merely a violation of an external rule but a rebellion against God himself, and it is the root of all the misery and evil in the world.
concepts: Sin as the transgression of the law of God
The object of sin is God; its essence is self-turning
Sin as personal act and as state of alienation
The biblical vocabulary: hamartia, avedia, anomia
topics.context: The doctrine of sin is the ground of the doctrine of holiness and of the need for grace.
topics.takeaway: Sin is rebellion against God — a turning of the will from him to self — and it is the root of all the world's misery.

topics.title: Original Sin and Actual Sin
topics.explanation: The doctrine of original sin holds that all men, as descendants of Adam, are born in a state of sin and under the guilt of the fall. Original sin has two aspects: the guilt of Adam's first sin, imputed to his posterity by virtue of federal headship, and the corruption of nature inherited from him. Actual sin is the personal transgression of the individual, the outward expression of the inward corruption.
