The Reformed doctrine holds that original sin is not merely the tendency to sin but a real state of alienation from God, so that 'the heart is deceitful above all things' (Jer 17:9). The doctrine explains the universality and the power of sin, and it stands against every Pelagian or semi-Pelagian optimism about the natural capacity of the will.
concepts: Original sin: the guilt of Adam imputed to posterity
The corruption of nature inherited from Adam
Actual sin as the personal expression of the corruption
The state of alienation that original sin denotes
topics.context: The doctrine of original sin was defined against Pelagius and Semipelagianism at the Councils of Carthage and Orange.
topics.takeaway: All men are born under the guilt and the corruption of the fall, so that the will is unable of itself to turn to God.

topics.title: The Consequences of the Fall
topics.explanation: The fall brought upon the race a manifold curse. Spiritually, man was cut off from communion with God and became alienated from him. Morally, he became corrupt in all his faculties — mind, will and affections. Physically, he was subject to decay and death. Existentially, he was cast out of the garden and became a stranger in a world that was cursed. The fall affected the whole of man and the whole of the world, so that 'the whole world lies under the power of the evil one' (1 John 5:19). The consequences of the fall are the ground of the Christian's view of the human condition and of the need for the redemption that alone can undo the work of the fall.
concepts: The spiritual consequence: alienation from God
The moral consequence: corruption of all the faculties
The physical consequence: decay and death
The universal extent of the fall's effects
topics.context: The doctrine of the consequences of the fall is the ground of the Christian view of the human condition.
topics.takeaway: The fall cut man off from God, corrupted his nature, and subjected him to death — affecting the whole of man and the whole of the world.

topics.title: Human Depravity and the Will of Man
topics.explanation: The doctrine of total depravity holds that the fall affected all the faculties of man, so that he is unable, of himself, to do anything that pleases God. This does not mean that man is as wicked as possible, but that the sin has reached every part of him — mind, will, affections. The will of the fallen man is not destroyed but bound: it freely chooses what it desires, but what it desires is always self, not God. The doctrine stands against the Pelagian and Arminian claim that the natural will can, of itself, choose the good and turn to God. Only the grace of the Spirit can liberate the will and turn it to God (John 6:44; 1 Cor 2:14).
concepts: Total depravity: the fall affected all the faculties
The will as bound, not destroyed
The free choice of self, not God
The need of grace to liberate the will
topics.context: The doctrine was defined at the Synod of Dort (1618-19) against the Arminian denial of the bondage of the will.
topics.takeaway: The fallen will is bound to self; only the grace of the Spirit can liberate it and turn it to God.

topics.title: The Unity and Dignity of Mankind
topics.explanation: The doctrine of man affirms both the unity and the dignity of the human race. All men are one race, created from the one man, Adam (Gen 2:7; Acts 17:26), and all share in the image of God, however marred. The unity of the race is the ground of the universal solidarity of mankind and of the equal dignity of every person. The dignity of man does not depend on race, sex, status or achievement, but on his being made in the image of God and on his being the object of God's redemptive love in Christ. The doctrine is the scriptural foundation of the modern affirmations of human rights and of the sanctity of human life.
concepts: The unity of the race from the one man, Adam
All men as bearers of the image of God
Dignity grounded in the image and in God's redemptive love
The ground of human rights and the sanctity of life
topics.context: The doctrine of the unity and dignity of mankind is the scriptural foundation of the modern human-rights movement.
topics.takeaway: All men are one race in the image of God, and their dignity does not depend on any earthly distinction.

topics.title: Man in Light of Creation and the Fall
topics.explanation: This topic brings the doctrine of man to a summary. Man is the crown of creation, made in the image of God and set to steward his world. He was created in innocence and in communion with God, but he fell, and the fall brought upon him and his posterity a state of sin and alienation. The man who stands before God is thus at once dignified and depraved — made in the image, yet corrupted by sin; the object of God's love, yet the author of his own misery. The doctrine of man thus prepares the way for the doctrine of salvation: the very dignity of man's original estate and the depth of his fall together show the need for, and the excellence of, the redemption that God has accomplished in Christ.
concepts: Man as the crown of creation and the bearer of the image
The twofold estate: innocence and the fall
The man before God as dignified and depraved
The doctrine of man as the preparation for the doctrine of salvation
topics.context: The doctrine of man is the pivot between the doctrines of creation and of salvation.
topics.takeaway: Man is at once dignified and depraved — made in the image and corrupted by sin — and so stands in need of the redemption that God has given in Christ.

ideas: Man is the crown of creation, made in the image of God as a unity of body and soul.
He was created in innocence under a covenant of works, in which Adam stood as federal head.
The fall brought upon the race the guilt and the corruption of sin, binding the will to self.
The man before God is thus at once dignified and depraved, and stands in need of redemption.
summary.connections: The doctrine of man explains the need for the redemption that the doctrines of Christ and of salvation will unfold; the image of God grounds the dignity of the person, and the fall grounds the necessity of grace.
summary.progression: Having seen the estate of man, the programme turns to the third person of the Trinity — the Holy Spirit, whose work is to accomplish the redemption that man's fall has made necessary.

modules.title: The Holy Spirit: The Doctrine of the Spirit
modules.divider_intro: The person, divinity and works of the third person of the Trinity in creation, redemption and the life of the believer.

intro.discipline: Pneumatology is the doctrine of the Holy Spirit: his person, his divinity, and his works in creation, in the life of Christ, in the world, and in the life of the believer. It is the doctrine that completes the triune God and that applies the redemption of Christ to the soul.
intro.context: The full doctrine of the Spirit emerged in the Church's experience and in the New Testament witness. The Spirit is named together with the Father and the Son in the baptismal formula, and the New Testament presents his work as the application of the work of Christ to the believer.
intro.relevance: The doctrine of the Spirit is the bridge between the objective work of Christ and the subjective experience of the believer. It is the ground of the Christian's assurance, of spiritual life and growth, and of the Church's power and unity.
intro.focus: To understand the person and divinity of the Spirit, and to trace his works from creation through the life of Christ to the sanctification and sealing of the believer.

topics.title: The Personhood of the Holy Spirit
topics.explanation: The Holy Spirit is a person, not an impersonal force or influence. The Scripture ascribes to him the personal attributes: he has a will (1 Cor 12:11), he knows (1 Cor 2:11), he speaks (Acts 8:29), he can be grieved (Eph 4:30), he intercedes (Rom 8:26), and he is called 'He' throughout the New Testament. He is the agent of divine acts — he creates, he inspires, he convicts, he regenerates, he sanctifies. The personhood of the Spirit is the ground of the Christian's personal relation to the third person of the Trinity and of the worship due to him as God.
concepts: The personal attributes ascribed to the Spirit
The Spirit as the agent of divine acts
The Spirit as 'He' throughout the New Testament
The ground of the personal relation to and worship of the Spirit
topics.context: The personhood of the Spirit was affirmed against the Pneumatomachians, who denied the full divinity of the Spirit.
topics.takeaway: The Holy Spirit is a person — he wills, knows, speaks and intercedes — and is to be related to and worshipped as such.

topics.title: The Divinity of the Holy Spirit
topics.explanation: The Holy Spirit is God. The Scripture ascribes to him the divine attributes: he is eternal (Heb 9:14), omnipresent (Ps 139:7), omniscient (1 Cor 2:10-11), and omnipotent. He is the agent of divine acts that only God can perform — creation (Gen 1:2), regeneration (Tit 3:5), and the raising of the dead (Rom 8:11). He is worshipped (Acts 5:3-4 equates lying to the Spirit with lying to God) and is named on equal terms with the Father and the Son in the baptismal formula and in the benedictions (Matt 28:19; 2 Cor 13:14). The divinity of the Spirit is the ground of the worship due to him and of the efficacy of his works.
concepts: The divine attributes ascribed to the Spirit
The Spirit as the agent of acts that only God can perform
The Spirit worshipped and named equal with the Father and the Son
The ground of the worship due to the Spirit
topics.context: The divinity of the Spirit was defined at Constantinople (381) against the Pneumatomachians.
topics.takeaway: The Holy Spirit is God, possessing the divine attributes and performing the divine acts, and is to be worshipped as such.

topics.title: The Work of the Spirit in Creation and the Old Testament
topics.explanation: The work of the Spirit extends over the whole of Scripture, from creation to the Church. In creation, 'the Spirit of God was moving over the face of the waters' (Gen 1:2). In the Old Testament, the Spirit came upon the judges, the prophets and the kings to empower them for their tasks (Num 11:25; 1 Sam 16:13; Judg 14:6). The Spirit is the agent of the inspiration of the Old Testament prophets (2 Pet 1:21) and the power behind the great acts of God in Israel's history. The Old Testament presents the Spirit's work as coming upon particular individuals for particular tasks, in anticipation of the fuller outpouring promised for the new covenant (Joel 2:28-32; Ezek 36:27).
concepts: The Spirit moving over the face of the waters in creation
The Spirit coming upon judges, prophets and kings
The Spirit as the agent of prophetic inspiration
The promise of the fuller outpouring in the new covenant
topics.context: The Old Testament doctrine of the Spirit anticipates the new-covenant outpouring promised by Joel and Ezekiel.
topics.takeaway: The Spirit is active throughout the Old Testament, empowering God's people and anticipating the fuller outpouring of the new covenant.

topics.title: The Spirit and the Life of Christ
topics.explanation: The Holy Spirit is the agent of the work of Christ at every stage. The Spirit oversadowed the virgin Mary in the incarnation (Luke 1:35). The Spirit anointed Jesus at his baptism (Matt 3:16) and led him into the wilderness (Matt 4:1). Jesus himself spoke of the Spirit as the one who would bear witness to him, would guide the apostles into all truth, and would glorify him (John 14:26; 16:13-14). The resurrection of Christ was the work of the Spirit of him who raised the Lord Jesus from the dead (Rom 1:4; 1 Cor 15:45). The Spirit thus unites the person and work of Christ to the life of the believer, applying to the soul what Christ has accomplished.
concepts: The Spirit in the incarnation, baptism and temptation of Christ
The Spirit as the witness to and glorifier of Christ
The Spirit as the agent of the resurrection
The Spirit applying the work of Christ to the believer
topics.context: The doctrine of the Spirit and Christ is the key to the unity of the person and work of the triune God in redemption.
topics.takeaway: The Spirit is the agent of the whole work of Christ, from the incarnation to the resurrection, applying it to the believer.

topics.title: The Descent of the Spirit at Pentecost
topics.explanation: Pentecost is the event in which the promised outpouring of the Spirit was fulfilled. On the day of Pentecost, 'suddenly there came a sound from heaven like a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And there appeared to them dividing tongues as of fire, and one sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit' (Acts 2:1-4). The outpouring marked the beginning of the Church and the inauguration of the new-covenant age. The Spirit came not merely upon particular individuals for particular tasks, as in the Old Testament, but upon the whole Church, the ground of its unity, its power, and its witness to the world.
concepts: The promise of the outpouring in Joel 2 and Acts 1
The signs: the wind, the tongues of fire, the filling
Pentecost as the beginning of the Church
The Spirit given to the whole Church, not only to individuals
topics.context: Pentecost is the scriptural event that inaugurates the new-covenant age and the age of the Church.
topics.takeaway: At Pentecost the promised Spirit was poured out upon the whole Church, marking the beginning of the new-covenant age.

topics.title: The Work of the Spirit in the World
topics.explanation: The Spirit is active in the world, though his saving work is not given to all. His general work in the world is to convict it of sin, of righteousness and of judgement (John 16:8-11). He bears witness to Christ, he restrains evil, and he gives the common grace that sustains the natural order. But his saving work — the effectual call, regeneration and the new birth — is given to the elect alone, in accordance with the decree of God. The distinction between the general and the special work of the Spirit is essential: the Spirit is the agent of common grace to all, but the agent of saving grace to the elect alone.
concepts: The conviction of the world: sin, righteousness, judgement
The bearing of witness to Christ
The common grace that sustains the natural order
The distinction between general and saving work
topics.context: The doctrine of the Spirit's work in the world is the ground of the Christian's view of common grace and of mission.
topics.takeaway: The Spirit convicts the world and sustains the natural order, but his saving work is given to the elect alone.

topics.title: The Work of the Spirit in Conversion and Regeneration
topics.explanation: Conversion is the turning of the sinner from sin to God, and it has two aspects: repentance and faith. Regeneration (the new birth) is the work of the Spirit in which the dead sinner is made alive in Christ (Eph 2:4-5; John 3:3-8). It is the root of conversion: the Spirit first regenerates the will, and the regenerated will then repents and believes. Regeneration is a monergistic work — it is the work of the Spirit alone, not a cooperation of the Spirit and the natural will. It is the ground of the new relationship to God, and it is the beginning of the Christian life. The doctrine is the scriptural answer to the question of how the dead sinner can turn to God.
concepts: Conversion as the twofold act of repentance and faith
Regeneration as the new birth, the root of conversion
The monergistic character of regeneration
Regeneration as the ground of the new relationship to God
topics.context: The doctrine of regeneration was at the centre of the Reformed-Arminian controversy over the nature of the new birth.
topics.takeaway: The Spirit regenerates the dead sinner, enabling the will to repent and believe; regeneration is the root of the Christian life.

topics.title: The Work of the Spirit in Sanctification
topics.explanation: Sanctification is the work of the Spirit in which the believer is made conformable to the image of Christ and holy in conduct. It is the continuing application of the work of Christ to the life of the believer, and it is the work of the Spirit throughout the whole of the Christian life. The Spirit sanctifies by the word of God (John 17:17), by the ordinances, and by the work of grace in the heart. Sanctification is progressive, not complete in this life, and it is the work of the Spirit in cooperation with the free effort of the believer. The goal of sanctification is the likeness of the Son, and it is the ground of the Christian's growth in grace and in good works.
concepts: Sanctification as conformity to the image of Christ
The means: the word, the ordinances, and the work of grace
The progressive and cooperative character of sanctification
The goal: the likeness of the Son
topics.context: The doctrine of sanctification is the ground of the Christian life and of the practice of spiritual discipline.
topics.takeaway: The Spirit sanctifies the believer progressively, conforming him to the image of Christ by the word and by the work of grace.

topics.title: The Gifts of the Holy Spirit
topics.explanation: The gifts of the Holy Spirit are the endowments of power and of ability that the Spirit gives to the members of the Church for the building up of the body of Christ and the service of the world. The classic list is given in 1 Corinthians 12:8-10: the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, faith, the working of miracles, prophecy, the distinguishing of spirits, tongues, and interpretation of tongues. The gifts are distributed by the Spirit 'as he wills' (1 Cor 12:11), and they are for the common good, not for private glory. The doctrine of the gifts is to be held in balance: they are real, they are for the edification of the Church, and they are to be exercised in order and in love.
concepts: The gifts as endowments for the building up of the Church
The list of 1 Corinthians 12:8-10
The distribution of the gifts 'as he wills'
The exercise of the gifts in order and in love
topics.context: The doctrine of the gifts is at the centre of the charismatic and the classic positions, and it is to be held in balance.
topics.takeaway: The gifts of the Spirit are endowments for the common good, distributed as he wills and exercised in order and in love.

topics.title: The Fruit of the Spirit
topics.explanation: The fruit of the Spirit is the character of Christ produced in the life of the believer by the work of the Spirit. Paul lists it in Galatians 5:22-23: 'love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance.' Unlike the gifts, which are endowments of ability, the fruit is the product of the Spirit's indwelling work in the heart. It is the evidence of the Spirit's presence and of the genuineness of the Christian life. The fruit is the ground of the Christian's testimony to the world and the mark of the mature believer. The doctrine of the fruit is the positive side of the doctrine of sanctification: it is the character that the Spirit produces in the life he has renewed.
concepts: The fruit as the character of Christ in the believer
The list of Galatians 5:22-23
The fruit as the evidence of the Spirit's presence
The fruit as the mark of the mature believer
topics.context: The fruit of the Spirit is the scriptural standard of Christian character and of the evidence of salvation.
topics.takeaway: The fruit of the Spirit is the character of Christ produced in the believer, the evidence of the Spirit's presence and the mark of maturity.

topics.title: The Baptism of the Holy Spirit
topics.explanation: The baptism of the Holy Spirit is the work of the Spirit in which the believer is united to Christ and to his body, the Church. It is distinct from the new birth in that it is the work of incorporation into the body of Christ, and it is the work of the Spirit in which the believer is sealed and marked as Christ's. The New Testament presents the baptism of the Spirit as a single, definitive act that unites all believers, Jew and Gentile, to the one body of Christ (1 Cor 12:13; Eph 4:4-6). The doctrine is the ground of the unity of the Church and of the believer's assurance of his place in the body of Christ. The various positions on the timing and the evidence of the baptism are to be held in the light of this scriptural doctrine.
concepts: The baptism as the work of incorporation into the body of Christ
The distinction from the new birth
The unity of the Church as the ground of the doctrine
The believer's assurance of his place in the body
topics.context: The doctrine of the baptism of the Spirit is at the centre of the charismatic and the classic positions.
topics.takeaway: The baptism of the Spirit unites the believer to Christ and to his body, the ground of the Church's unity and the believer's assurance.

topics.title: The Spirit as Seal and Guarantee of the Believer
topics.explanation: The Holy Spirit is the seal and the guarantee (earnest) of the believer's salvation. As a seal, the Spirit marks the believer as God's own, the token of ownership and of security (Eph 1:13-14; 2 Cor 1:21-22). As a guarantee, the Spirit is the down-payment of the inheritance, the firstfruits of the glory to come (Rom 8:23; Eph 1:14). The seal and the guarantee are the ground of the Christian's assurance of salvation and of his hope of the inheritance. The doctrine is the comfort of the believer: the same Spirit who has begun the good work will also complete it (Phil 1:6).
concepts: The Spirit as seal: the token of ownership and security
The Spirit as guarantee: the down-payment of the inheritance
The ground of the assurance of salvation
The hope of the inheritance to come
topics.context: The doctrine of the Spirit as seal and guarantee is the ground of the Christian's assurance and hope.
topics.takeaway: The Spirit seals and guarantees the believer's salvation, the ground of his assurance and of his hope of the inheritance.

ideas: The Holy Spirit is a person and is fully God, to be related to and worshipped as such.
The Spirit is the agent of the whole work of Christ, from creation and the incarnation to the resurrection.
At Pentecost the Spirit was poured out upon the whole Church, inaugurating the new-covenant age.
The Spirit regenerates, sanctifies, gifts, seals and guarantees the believer, applying the work of Christ to the soul.
summary.connections: The doctrine of the Spirit completes the triune God and is the bridge between the objective work of Christ and the subjective life of the believer; it grounds the Church's unity, power and the Christian's assurance.
summary.progression: Having seen the triune God in his works of creation and redemption, the programme turns to the centre of the whole: the person and work of Jesus Christ.

modules.title: Christology: The Person and Work of Christ
modules.divider_intro: The person, natures, life, death, resurrection, ascension and present ministry of the Lord Jesus Christ.

intro.discipline: Christology is the doctrine of the person and work of Jesus Christ: his person, his two natures, his life, his death as the atonement, his resurrection, his ascension, and his present ministry at the right hand of God. It is the central doctrine of the Christian faith.
intro.context: Christology is the doctrine around which the whole of the faith is constructed. The councils of Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451) defined the person and natures of Christ, and the confession of the faith centres on him.
intro.relevance: The person of Christ is the ground of the whole redemption. Whatever the Church says about salvation, about the Spirit, and about the last things is controlled by what it says about Christ. Christology is the doctrinal centre of the entire programme.
intro.focus: To articulate the person, natures, life, atoning death, resurrection, ascension and present ministry of Christ as Scripture and the creeds confess them.

topics.title: The Person of Christ
topics.explanation: The person of Christ is the subject of the whole doctrine of redemption. Jesus of Nazareth is not merely a great teacher or a prophet, but the eternal Son of God made man — the God-man, the mediator between God and man (1 Tim 2:5; Heb 3:6). The person of Christ is one divine person, the second person of the Trinity, who assumed a complete human nature in the incarnation. The confession of the person of Christ is the confession that Jesus is Lord (Phil 2:11) and that in him the whole of God's purpose of redemption is accomplished. The person of Christ is thus the ground of the faith and the object of its worship.
concepts: Christ as the eternal Son of God made man
The one divine person, the second person of the Trinity
Christ as the mediator between God and man
The confession that Jesus is Lord
topics.context: The person of Christ was defined at Nicaea (325) against Arianism and at Chalcedon (451) against the natures controversies.
topics.takeaway: The person of Christ is the one divine person who assumed a complete human nature — the ground and object of the whole faith.

topics.title: The Pre-Existence of Christ
topics.explanation: The pre-existence of Christ is the doctrine that the Son of God existed before his incarnation, in eternal relation with the Father. The New Testament is explicit: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1). The Son is the agent of creation (John 1:3; Col 1:16), the upholder of the universe (Heb 1:3), and the one through whom all things were made. The Old Testament anticipates the pre-existence in the 'Angel of the LORD' and in the wisdom and counsel passages. The doctrine of the pre-existence is the ground of the deity of Christ and of his role as the agent of creation and the mediator of redemption.
concepts: The Word 'in the beginning' with God and as God
The Son as the agent of creation and the upholder of the universe
The Old Testament anticipations: the Angel of the LORD, wisdom
The ground of the deity of Christ
topics.context: The doctrine of the pre-existence was affirmed at Nicaea against Arianism, which denied the eternal existence of the Son.
topics.takeaway: The Son of God existed before the incarnation, as the agent of creation and the eternal Word, the ground of his deity.

topics.title: The Names and Titles of Christ
topics.explanation: The Scripture gives Christ a rich vocabulary of names and titles that express the fullness of his person and work. He is the Word (John 1:1), the Wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24), the Image of the invisible God (Col 1:15), the Angel of the LORD, the Son of God, the Son of Man, the Messiah, the Lord, the King of Kings, and the Root and Offspring of David. The title 'Son of God' expresses his divine sonship and his unique relation to the Father. The title 'Son of Man' expresses his true humanity and his coming in the glory of his kingdom (Dan 7:13-14). The titles together present the fullness of the person and work of Christ.
concepts: The Word, the Wisdom, the Image of the invisible God
The titles: Son of God, Son of Man, Messiah, Lord
The Son of God: divine sonship and unique relation to the Father
The Son of Man: true humanity and the coming in glory
topics.context: The titles of Christ are the scriptural vocabulary of the high and the low Christology.
topics.takeaway: The names and titles of Christ together express the fullness of his person — the eternal Word made the true Son of Man.

topics.title: The Virgin Birth of Christ
topics.explanation: The virgin birth is the doctrine that the human nature of Christ was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary, without human seed (Matt 1:18-25; Luke 1:26-38). The doctrine is affirmed by all four Gospels and is the ground of the true humanity of Christ: he is the true son of David by the line of Joseph and the true son of Mary. The virgin birth is also the ground of the sinlessness of Christ: he was not born into the corrupt lineage of Adam but was the seed of the woman (Gal 4:4; 2 Tim 2:8). The doctrine was affirmed at the early councils and is a necessary part of the confession of the incarnation.
concepts: Conception by the Holy Spirit, birth of the virgin Mary
The ground of the true humanity and the sinlessness of Christ
The Son of David and the Son of God in one person
The affirmation of the early councils
topics.context: The virgin birth was affirmed at the early councils and is a necessary part of the confession of the incarnation.
topics.takeaway: The virgin birth is the ground of the true humanity and the sinlessness of Christ, the seed of the woman in whom the promise was fulfilled.

topics.title: The Two Natures of Christ and the Hypostatic Union
topics.explanation: The doctrine of the two natures of Christ confesses that in the one person of the Son of God there are two complete, distinct natures — divine and human — united without confusion, change, division or separation. This is the hypostatic union, defined at the Council of Chalcedon (451). The divine nature is not changed into the human, nor the human into the divine; the two are not mixed, nor separated into two persons. The communication of attributes (communicatio idiomatum) is the doctrine that the properties of each nature are predicated of the one person. The doctrine is the guard against the Arian, Nestorian, Eutychian and Monophysite heresies, and it is the ground of the mediatorial work of Christ.
concepts: Two complete natures: divine and human
The hypostatic union: without confusion, change, division or separation
The communication of attributes (communicatio idiomatum)
The guard against the Arian, Nestorian and Eutychian heresies
topics.context: The doctrine was defined at Chalcedon (451) in response to the Monophysite and Nestorian controversies.
topics.takeaway: In the one person of Christ there are two complete natures, divine and human, united without confusion, change, division or separation.

topics.title: The Life and Ministry of Christ
topics.explanation: The life and ministry of Christ span the three years of his public work, from the baptism in the Jordan to the crucifixion. His ministry was threefold: he taught, he worked miracles, and he proclaimed the kingdom of God. His teaching was that of authority, 'as one having authority, and not as the scribes' (Matt 7:29). His miracles were the signs of the kingdom and the demonstration of his divine power. His proclamation was the good news of the kingdom of God, the nearness of the reign of God, and the call to repentance and faith. The life and ministry of Christ are the demonstration of his person and the ground of the apostolic witness.
concepts: The threefold ministry: teaching, miracles, proclamation
The teaching of authority
The miracles as the signs of the kingdom
The proclamation of the kingdom of God
topics.context: The ministry of Christ is the demonstration of his person and the ground of the apostolic witness and of the faith.
topics.takeaway: The life and ministry of Christ — his teaching, his miracles, his proclamation — are the demonstration of his person and the ground of the faith.

topics.title: The Teachings of Christ: The Kingdom of God
topics.explanation: The central theme of the teaching of Christ is the kingdom of God. The kingdom is the reign of God, the rule of God over all things, which was drawn near in the person and work of Christ. The kingdom is at once a present reality — 'the kingdom of God is at hand' (Mark 1:15) — and a future consummation — the coming of the kingdom in power at the second advent. The teachings of Christ on the kingdom include the parables, the beatitudes, and the lord's prayer. The kingdom is the framework within which the whole of the teaching of Christ is to be understood, and it is the ground of the Church's hope and of its mission.
concepts: The kingdom as the reign and the rule of God
The kingdom as present reality and future consummation
The parables, the beatitudes and the lord's prayer
The kingdom as the framework of the teaching of Christ
topics.context: The kingdom of God is the central theme of the Synoptic Gospels and the framework of the teaching of Christ.
topics.takeaway: The kingdom of God — the reign of God drawn near in Christ — is the central theme of the teaching of Christ and the ground of the Church's hope.

topics.title: The Miracles of Christ
topics.explanation: The miracles of Christ are the supernatural acts by which he demonstrated his divine power and the reality of the kingdom. The Gospels record over thirty miracles, including the raising of the dead, the healing of the sick, the stilling of the storm, and the feeding of the multitudes. The miracles are not mere exhibitions of power but the signs of the kingdom and the demonstration of the compassion of Christ. They are the ground of the faith of the disciples and the evidence of the deity of Christ. The doctrine of the miracles is to be held in balance: they are real, they are the signs of the kingdom, and they are not to be separated from the teaching and the person of Christ.
concepts: The miracles as the signs of the kingdom
The raising of the dead, the healings, the nature miracles
The demonstration of the compassion and the deity of Christ
The ground of the faith of the disciples
topics.context: The miracles of Christ are the demonstration of his divine power and the ground of the apostolic witness.
topics.takeaway: The miracles of Christ are the signs of the kingdom and the demonstration of his compassion and deity, the ground of the faith.

topics.title: The Doctrine of the Atonement: General Principles
topics.explanation: The atonement is the work of Christ by which he reconciles sinners to God. The general principles of the atonement are: it is the work of the God-man, the mediator; it is the work of the whole person of Christ, not merely his human nature; it is accomplished by his death, his burial and his resurrection; and it is the ground of the reconciliation of the sinner to God. The atonement is both objective — the work by which God is satisfied and the sinner reconciled — and subjective — the application of that work to the believer by the Spirit. The doctrine of the atonement is the heart of the gospel and the ground of the whole of the Christian faith.
concepts: The atonement as the work of the God-man, the mediator
The work of the whole person of Christ
Accomplished by death, burial and resurrection
The objective and the subjective aspects of the atonement
topics.context: The doctrine of the atonement is the heart of the gospel and the ground of the whole of the Christian faith.
topics.takeaway: The atonement is the work of the God-man by which he reconciles sinners to God, the heart of the gospel and the ground of the faith.

topics.title: The Nature of Christ's Death as a Sacrifice
topics.explanation: The death of Christ is a sacrifice — the offering of himself to God as the propitiation for sin (Rom 3:25; 1 John 2:2). The sacrificial language of the New Testament is drawn from the Old Testament system of sacrifice, in which the blood of the victim was the means of the atonement. Christ is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29), the Passover lamb (1 Cor 5:7), the high priest who offers himself (Heb 9:11-14). The sacrifice of Christ is once for all, perfect and sufficient, and it is the ground of the new covenant. The doctrine of the sacrifice is the scriptural foundation of the atonement and the ground of the believer's approach to God.
concepts: The death of Christ as the propitiation for sin
The sacrificial language drawn from the Old Testament
Christ as the Lamb of God and the Passover lamb
The once-for-all, perfect and sufficient sacrifice
topics.context: The doctrine of the sacrifice of Christ is the scriptural foundation of the atonement, drawn from the Old Testament system of sacrifice.
topics.takeaway: The death of Christ is a sacrifice — the offering of himself as the propitiation for sin, once for all, perfect and sufficient.

topics.title: The Major Theories of the Atonement
topics.explanation: The Church has developed several theories of the atonement, each emphasizing a different aspect of the work of Christ. The ransom theory presents the atonement as the payment of a ransom to liberate the captive sinner. The moral-influence theory presents the atonement as the demonstration of the love of God that moves the sinner to repentance. The satisfaction theory (Anselm) presents the atonement as the satisfaction of the honour of God. The penal-substitution theory presents the atonement as the bearing of the penalty of sin in the place of the sinner. The great councils and the Reformed confessions affirm the penal-substitutionary aspect as the central meaning of the atonement, while acknowledging the other aspects as genuine but secondary. The responsible position is to hold the whole of the atonement, with the penal-substitutionary aspect at its centre.
concepts: The ransom theory: liberation of the captive sinner
The moral-influence theory: the demonstration of the love of God
The satisfaction theory (Anselm): the satisfaction of the honour of God
The penal-substitution theory: the bearing of the penalty in the sinner's place
topics.context: The theories of the atonement were developed from the early Church (Chrysostom, Anselm) to the Reformation (Luther, Calvin).
topics.takeaway: The atonement has several genuine aspects, but its centre is the penal-substitutionary bearing of the penalty of sin in the sinner's place.

topics.title: Substitution and Penal Satisfaction in the Atonement
topics.explanation: The doctrine of penal substitution holds that Christ, in his death, bore the penalty of sin in the place of the sinner, satisfying the justice of God and making it possible for God to be just and the justifier of the one who believes (Rom 3:26). The substitution is real: Christ stood in the place of the sinner, 'he made him to be sin who knew no sin, that we might become the righteousness of God in him' (2 Cor 5:21). The penal satisfaction is the satisfaction of the justice of God: the penalty due to the sinner was borne by the Son, and the justice of God was satisfied. The doctrine is the ground of the assurance of the believer and of the confidence that the righteousness of God is not compromised by the pardon of the sinner.
concepts: The substitution: Christ standing in the place of the sinner
The penal satisfaction: the satisfaction of the justice of God
The ground of the assurance of the believer
The reconciliation of the justice and the mercy of God
topics.context: The doctrine of penal substitution was the central doctrine of the Reformation and is affirmed in the Reformed confessions.
topics.takeaway: In his death Christ bore the penalty of sin in the sinner's place, satisfying the justice of God and making possible the pardon of the believer.

topics.title: The Resurrection of Christ
topics.explanation: The resurrection of Christ is the raising of the crucified Lord from the dead by the power of the Father. It is the vindication of the person and work of Christ, the demonstration of his victory over sin and death, and the ground of the hope of the believer. The New Testament is explicit that Christ 'was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures' (1 Cor 15:4), and that his resurrection is the 'firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep' (1 Cor 15:20). The resurrection is not a mere resuscitation but the entrance of the person of Christ into a new mode of existence — the glorified, risen life. The doctrine of the resurrection is the ground of the Christian hope and the demonstration of the power of God.
concepts: The resurrection as the vindication of the person and work of Christ
The demonstration of the victory over sin and death
The firstfruits of the resurrection of the dead
The entrance into the glorified, risen life
topics.context: The resurrection is the central event of the Christian faith and the ground of the hope of the believer.
topics.takeaway: The resurrection of Christ is the vindication of his work, the victory over sin and death, and the firstfruits of the hope of the believer.

topics.title: The Ascension of Christ
topics.explanation: The ascension of Christ is the bodily ascent of the risen Lord into heaven, at the right hand of God. It is the completion of the humiliation and the exaltation of Christ, and it is the ground of his present session and intercession. The New Testament records the ascension (Acts 1:9-11) and the session at the right hand of the Father (Eph 1:20; Heb 1:3). The ascension is the ground of the Church's confidence that Christ is now in heaven, interceding for his people and preparing a place for them (John 14:2-3). The doctrine of the ascension is the bridge between the resurrection and the present ministry of Christ, and it is the ground of the Church's hope of its own ascent.
concepts: The bodily ascent of the risen Lord into heaven
The completion of the humiliation and the exaltation
The ground of the present session and intercession
The preparation of a place for the Church
topics.context: The ascension is the completion of the work of Christ and the ground of his present ministry at the right hand of God.
topics.takeaway: The ascension of Christ is the completion of his exaltation, the ground of his present intercession, and the hope of the Church's own ascent.

topics.title: The Present Session and Intercession of Christ
topics.explanation: The present session of Christ is his enthronement at the right hand of the Father, in heaven, where he reigns over all things and intercedes for his people. The session is the ground of the Church's confidence that Christ is now active in her behalf, and the intercession is the ground of the assurance of the believer. The New Testament presents Christ as the high priest who 'ever lives to make intercession for us' (Heb 7:25) and as the mediator who 'always intercedes' for his people (Rom 8:34). The present ministry of Christ is the application of the work of the atonement to the life of the Church, and it is the ground of the Christian's confidence in prayer and in the trial.
concepts: The session at the right hand of the Father
The reign of Christ over all things
The intercession for his people
The application of the atonement to the life of the Church
topics.context: The present ministry of Christ is the application of the atonement to the life of the Church and the ground of the Christian's confidence.
topics.takeaway: Christ now reigns at the right hand of the Father and intercedes for his people, the ground of the Church's confidence and the Christian's assurance.

topics.title: The Second Coming of Christ
topics.explanation: The second coming of Christ is the doctrine that the risen and ascended Lord will come again, visibly and in power, to judge the living and the dead and to consummate the kingdom of God. The New Testament is explicit that 'the Lord himself will descend from heaven' (1 Thess 4:16) and that he will come 'in glory' (Matt 25:31). The second coming is the ground of the Christian hope and the motivation of the Christian life. The doctrine is to be held in balance: it is certain, it is the goal of the Church's hope, and it is the motivation of the Christian's witness and of his holy living. The doctrine of the second coming is the eschatological counterpart of the incarnation: as Christ came in humility, so he will come in glory.
concepts: The visible, personal and certain return of the Lord
The coming in power to judge the living and the dead
The consummation of the kingdom of God
The ground of the Christian hope and the motivation of the life
topics.context: The second coming is the eschatological counterpart of the incarnation and the ground of the Christian hope.
topics.takeaway: The Lord Jesus will come again, visibly and in power, to judge the world and to consummate the kingdom — the ground of the Christian hope.

ideas: Christ is the eternal Son of God made man — one person in two complete natures, the hypostatic union.
His life and ministry were the demonstration of his person: teaching, miracles, and the proclamation of the kingdom.
His death was the atoning sacrifice, bearing the penalty of sin in the sinner's place and satisfying the justice of God.
His resurrection, ascension and present session are the ground of the Church's hope and the Christian's assurance.
summary.connections: The person and work of Christ are the ground of the whole redemption: the atonement is the heart of the gospel, and the present ministry of Christ applies it to the life of the Church. The doctrines of the Spirit, of salvation and of the last things all flow from the person and work of Christ.
summary.progression: Having seen the person and work of Christ, the programme turns to the application of that work to the sinner: the doctrine of salvation.

modules.title: Soteriology: The Doctrine of Salvation
modules.divider_intro: The application of the work of Christ to the sinner: election, grace, faith, justification, sanctification and glorification.

intro.discipline: Soteriology is the doctrine of salvation: the application of the work of Christ to the sinner, from election to glorification. It treats the order of salvation (ordo salutis) — the works of grace by which the believer is brought from death to life, from condemnation to justification, and from sin to holiness.
intro.context: The doctrine of salvation is the heart of the gospel and the ground of the Christian's assurance. The New Testament presents salvation as the work of God, accomplished in Christ, applied by the Spirit, and received by faith.
intro.relevance: The doctrine of salvation is the ground of the Christian's assurance and of the Church's witness. It answers the question, 'How is the sinner saved?' and it is the motivation of the Christian life and of the Church's mission.
intro.focus: To understand the order of salvation — election, faith, justification, sanctification, glorification — as the application of the work of Christ to the sinner.

topics.title: The General Doctrine of Salvation
topics.explanation: The general doctrine of salvation confesses that salvation is the work of God, accomplished in Christ and applied by the Spirit, and received by faith. It is not the work of the sinner but the gift of God (Eph 2:8-9). The salvation of God is the redemption of the sinner from the power and the penalty of sin, and the restoration of the sinner to the favour of God and to the life of holiness. The doctrine is grounded in the work of Christ — his death, his burial and his resurrection — and it is applied to the sinner by the work of the Spirit. The general doctrine is the framework within which the particular works of grace are to be understood.
concepts: Salvation as the work of God, the gift of grace
Accomplished in Christ and applied by the Spirit
Received by faith
The redemption from the power and the penalty of sin
topics.context: The general doctrine of salvation is the framework of the whole of the soteriological teaching of the New Testament.
topics.takeaway: Salvation is the work of God, accomplished in Christ and applied by the Spirit, and received by faith — the gift of grace.

topics.title: Election and Predestination
topics.explanation: Election is the doctrine that God, from eternity, chose in Christ some to be the objects of his saving grace. Predestination is the wider doctrine that God, from eternity, ordained all that comes to pass, and that the election of the sinner is the application of that decree to the work of redemption. The Reformed doctrine holds that the election is unconditional — it is not grounded on any foreseen merit or faith in the sinner, but on the free and sovereign purpose of God (Rom 9:11-16; Eph 1:4-5). The doctrine is the ground of the assurance of the believer and of the confidence that the purpose of God cannot be frustrated.
concepts: The election of some in Christ to saving grace
Predestination as the wider decree of God
The unconditional character of the election
The ground of the assurance of the believer
topics.context: The doctrine of election was at the centre of the Reformed-Arminian controversy and was defined at the Synod of Dort (1618-19).
topics.takeaway: God, from eternity, chose in Christ some to be the objects of his saving grace, the ground of the assurance of the believer.

topics.title: The Effectual Call and the Work of Grace
topics.explanation: The effectual call is the work of the Spirit by which he draws the sinner to Christ and enables him to respond in faith. It is distinct from the general call, which goes out to all through the proclamation of the gospel, in that the effectual call is given to the elect alone and is invariably successful. The effectual call is the work of grace in which the Spirit opens the closed heart, enlightens the darkened mind, and renews the will (Ezek 36:26-27; 2 Cor 4:6). The work of grace is monergistic: it is the work of the Spirit alone, not a cooperation of the Spirit and the natural will. The effectual call is the beginning of the subjective application of the work of Christ.
concepts: The distinction between the general and the effectual call
The work of the Spirit in opening the heart and renewing the will
The monergistic character of the work of grace
The beginning of the subjective application of the work of Christ
topics.context: The doctrine of the effectual call was defined at the Synod of Dort against the Arminian denial of the irresistible work of grace.
topics.takeaway: The effectual call is the work of the Spirit in which he draws the sinner to Christ and enables him to respond in faith.

topics.title: Faith as the Instrument of Salvation
topics.explanation: Faith is the instrument by which the sinner receives the salvation that God has prepared in Christ. Faith is not a work that merits salvation but the empty hand that receives the gift. It has three aspects: the knowledge of the truth (notitia), the assent to the truth (assensus), and the personal trust and reliance on Christ (fiducia). The third, fiducia, is the proper work of the Spirit and the distinguishing mark of saving faith. Faith is the ground of the justification of the sinner (Rom 5:1) and the beginning of the Christian life. The doctrine of faith is the scriptural answer to the question of how the sinner is justified before God.
concepts: Faith as the instrument, not the meritorious cause, of salvation
The three aspects: notitia, assensus, fiducia
The fiducia as the proper work of the Spirit
The ground of the justification of the sinner
topics.context: The doctrine of faith was the centre of the Reformation's doctrine of justification by faith alone.
topics.takeaway: Faith is the instrument by which the sinner receives the salvation prepared in Christ — knowledge, assent, and personal trust in him.

topics.title: Repentance and Its Relation to Faith
topics.explanation: Repentance is the turning of the sinner from sin to God, and it is the necessary companion of faith. Repentance has two aspects: the sorrow for sin (contrition) and the turning from sin to God (conversion). It is not a mere regret but a change of mind and of will, a turning of the whole person from self to God. Repentance and faith are two aspects of the one work of grace: faith receives Christ, and repentance turns from sin. The two are inseparable, and the doctrine of repentance is the ground of the Christian's holy living and of the Church's call to holiness.
concepts: Repentance as the turning from sin to God
The two aspects: contrition and conversion
The inseparability of repentance and faith
The ground of the Christian's holy living
topics.context: The doctrine of repentance is the ground of the Christian's holy living and of the Church's call to holiness.
topics.takeaway: Repentance is the turning from sin to God, the inseparable companion of faith, and the ground of the Christian's holy living.

topics.title: Justification by Faith
topics.explanation: Justification is the act of God by which he declares the sinner to be righteous in his sight, on the ground of the righteousness of Christ imputed to him. It is a forensic, not a moral, act: God does not make the sinner righteous in the sense of infusing righteousness, but he declares him righteous on the ground of the imputed righteousness of Christ. Justification is by faith alone, through grace alone, on the ground of Christ alone (sola fide, sola gratia, solus Christus). It is the ground of the assurance of the believer and of his peace with God (Rom 5:1). The doctrine of justification was the centre of the Reformation and is the ground of the Christian's confidence before God.
concepts: Justification as a forensic declaration of righteousness
The imputation of the righteousness of Christ
By faith alone, through grace alone, on the ground of Christ alone
The ground of the assurance and the peace with God
topics.context: The doctrine of justification by faith was the centre of the Reformation and the ground of the Christian's confidence before God.
topics.takeaway: Justification is the act of God by which he declares the sinner righteous on the ground of the imputed righteousness of Christ, by faith alone.

topics.title: Adoption into the Family of God
topics.explanation: Adoption is the act of God by which he receives the justified sinner into the family of God, as his son or daughter, and gives him the full rights and privileges of that family. Adoption is the ground of the believer's sonship, and it is the basis of his call to 'Abba, Father' (Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6). The believer, as the adopted son, has the right to the inheritance, the right to the care of the Father, and the right to the intercession of the Spirit (Rom 8:26-27). Adoption is the ground of the Christian's confidence in prayer and of his hope of the inheritance. The doctrine of adoption is the personal side of the doctrine of justification.
concepts: Adoption as the reception into the family of God
The rights and privileges of the adopted son
The right to the inheritance and to the care of the Father
The ground of the confidence in prayer and of the hope
topics.context: The doctrine of adoption is the personal side of the doctrine of justification and the ground of the Christian's sonship.
topics.takeaway: Adoption is the reception of the justified sinner into the family of God, the ground of his sonship, his inheritance and his confidence in prayer.

topics.title: Regeneration and the New Birth
topics.explanation: Regeneration is the work of the Spirit in which the dead sinner is made alive in Christ, and it is the new birth (John 3:3-8). It is the root of the whole of the subjective application of the work of Christ, for it is the work that makes the sinner able to respond to the call of God. Regeneration is a monergistic work — it is the work of the Spirit alone — and it is the ground of the new relationship to God and of the new life. The new birth is the beginning of the Christian life, and it is the ground of the Christian's holiness and of his growth in grace. The doctrine of regeneration is the scriptural answer to the question of how the dead sinner can live.
concepts: Regeneration as the new birth, the making alive in Christ
The monergistic character of the work
The ground of the new relationship to God
The beginning of the Christian life and of the new holiness
topics.context: The doctrine of regeneration is the ground of the Christian's holiness and of his growth in grace.
topics.takeaway: Regeneration is the new birth, the work of the Spirit in which the dead sinner is made alive in Christ, the root of the Christian life.

topics.title: Sanctification: The Process of Being Made Holy
topics.explanation: Sanctification is the work of the Spirit in which the believer is made conformable to the image of Christ and holy in conduct. It is the continuing application of the work of Christ to the life of the believer, and it is the work of the Spirit throughout the whole of the Christian life. Sanctification is progressive, not complete in this life, and it is the work of the Spirit in cooperation with the free effort of the believer. The means of sanctification are the word of God, the ordinances, and the work of grace in the heart. The goal of sanctification is the likeness of the Son, and it is the ground of the Christian's growth in grace and in good works.
concepts: Sanctification as conformity to the image of Christ
The progressive and cooperative character of the work
The means: the word, the ordinances, and the work of grace
The goal: the likeness of the Son
topics.context: The doctrine of sanctification is the ground of the Christian life and of the practice of spiritual discipline.
topics.takeaway: Sanctification is the work of the Spirit in which the believer is made holy, progressively, by the word and by the work of grace.

topics.title: The Christian Life and Spiritual Growth
topics.explanation: The Christian life is the life of the believer in Christ, and it is the outworking of the salvation that God has accomplished. Spiritual growth is the process by which the believer is conformed more and more to the image of Christ, and it is the work of the Spirit in cooperation with the free effort of the believer. The means of spiritual growth are the word of God, prayer, the ordinances, and the fellowship of the saints. The Christian life is marked by the fruit of the Spirit, by the growth in grace, and by the good works that are the evidence of the faith. The doctrine of the Christian life is the practical side of the doctrine of sanctification, and it is the ground of the Christian's daily walk.
concepts: The Christian life as the life in Christ
Spiritual growth as conformity to the image of Christ
The means: the word, prayer, the ordinances, and fellowship
The marks: the fruit of the Spirit, the growth in grace, the good works
topics.context: The doctrine of the Christian life is the practical side of the doctrine of sanctification and the ground of the daily walk.
topics.takeaway: The Christian life is the outworking of salvation, marked by growth in grace, the fruit of the Spirit, and the good works of the faith.

topics.title: The Perseverance of the Saints
topics.explanation: The perseverance of the saints is the doctrine that the elect, having been regenerated and justified by God, will persevere in the faith to the end, and that none of them will finally fall away. The doctrine is grounded in the sovereign grace of God, the security of the believer in Christ, and the promise of God that he who began the good work will also complete it (Phil 1:6). The believer is kept by the power of God (1 Pet 1:5) and is sealed by the Spirit (Eph 1:13-14). The doctrine is the ground of the assurance of the believer and of his confidence in the trial. It is to be distinguished from the Antinomian abuse that uses it to excuse sin.
concepts: The perseverance of the elect to the end
The ground: the sovereign grace and the security in Christ
The keeping by the power of God and the sealing by the Spirit
The ground of the assurance and the confidence in the trial
topics.context: The doctrine of the perseverance of the saints was defined at the Synod of Dort and is a ground of the assurance of the believer.
topics.takeaway: The elect will persevere in the faith to the end, kept by the power of God — the ground of the assurance of the believer.

topics.title: The Assurance of Salvation
topics.explanation: The assurance of salvation is the confident conviction of the believer that he is in Christ and that his salvation is secure. It is the work of the Spirit, who bears witness with the spirit of the believer that he is a child of God (Rom 8:16). The ground of the assurance is the work of Christ, the promise of God, and the evidence of the Spirit's work in the life of the believer. The assurance is not a single experience but a growing confidence, and it is the ground of the Christian's joy and of his confidence in the trial. The doctrine of the assurance is the comfort of the believer and the ground of his worship.
concepts: The assurance as the work of the Spirit's witness
The ground: the work of Christ, the promise, and the evidence
The assurance as a growing confidence
The ground of the joy and the confidence in the trial
topics.context: The doctrine of the assurance of salvation is the comfort of the believer and the ground of his worship.
topics.takeaway: The assurance of salvation is the confident conviction that the believer is in Christ, the work of the Spirit and the comfort of the life.

topics.title: Justification and Sanctification Distinguished
topics.explanation: Justification and sanctification are two distinct but inseparable aspects of the salvation of God. Justification is the forensic act of God in which he declares the sinner righteous on the ground of the imputed righteousness of Christ; it is instantaneous and complete. Sanctification is the moral work of the Spirit in which the believer is made holy in conduct; it is progressive and incomplete in this life. The two are distinct in their nature, their manner and their completion, but they are inseparable in the experience of the believer: the justified are sanctified, and the sanctified are justified. The distinction is the guard against the confusion of the forensic and the moral, and it is the ground of the Christian's confidence and of his holy living.
concepts: Justification as the forensic, instantaneous act
Sanctification as the moral, progressive work
The distinction in nature, manner and completion
The inseparability in the experience of the believer
topics.context: The distinction between justification and sanctification is the guard against the confusion of the forensic and the moral.
topics.takeaway: Justification is the forensic declaration of righteousness; sanctification is the moral making holy — distinct but inseparable in the believer.

topics.title: Glorification
topics.explanation: Glorification is the final work of God in which the believer is made conformable to the body of the glory of Christ, and is made perfect in holiness. It is the completion of the salvation that began in the election and was applied in the justification and the sanctification. Glorification is the resurrection of the body and the perfection of the soul, and it is the entrance of the believer into the full possession of the inheritance (Rom 8:29-30; 1 Cor 15:42-44). The doctrine of glorification is the ground of the Christian hope and of his confidence in the death and in the resurrection. It is the final work of the ordo salutis.

The resurrection of the body and the perfection of the soul
The full possession of the inheritance
The ground of the Christian hope and the final work of the ordo salutis
topics.context: The doctrine of glorification is the final work of the ordo salutis and the ground of the Christian hope.
topics.takeaway: Glorification is the final work of God in which the believer is made perfect in holiness and enters the full possession of the inheritance.

topics.title: The Ground and Basis of Salvation
topics.explanation: The ground and basis of salvation is the work of Christ — his death, his burial and his resurrection. It is not the work of the sinner, not the merit of the Church, and not the power of the sacraments, but the work of Christ alone. The righteousness that is the ground of the justification of the sinner is the righteousness of Christ, imputed to him (2 Cor 5:21). The blood of Christ is the ground of the pardon of sin (1 John 1:7), and the resurrection of Christ is the ground of the hope of the believer (Rom 4:25). The doctrine of the ground of salvation is the guard against every form of works-righteousness and the ground of the Christian's confidence that his salvation is secure in Christ.
concepts: The ground of salvation is the work of Christ alone
The imputed righteousness of Christ
The blood of Christ as the ground of the pardon
The resurrection of Christ as the ground of the hope
topics.context: The doctrine of the ground of salvation is the guard against works-righteousness and the ground of the Christian's confidence.
topics.takeaway: The ground and basis of salvation is the work of Christ alone — his death, his burial and his resurrection — and not the work of the sinner.

topics.title: The Order of Salvation in Summary
topics.explanation: The order of salvation (ordo salutis) is the logical and the temporal order of the works of grace by which the believer is brought from death to life. The classical Reformed order is: the election, the effectual call, regeneration, faith, justification, adoption, sanctification, perseverance, and glorification. The order is a logical order, not a strict temporal sequence, for some of the works are simultaneous in the experience of the believer. The doctrine of the order of salvation is the framework within which the particular works of grace are to be understood, and it is the ground of the Christian's confidence that the work of God in him is orderly and complete. The order of salvation is the summary of the whole of the doctrine of salvation.
concepts: The ordo salutis: the logical and temporal order of the works of grace
The classical Reformed order
The logical order, not a strict temporal sequence
The framework of the doctrine of salvation
topics.context: The doctrine of the order of salvation is the summary of the whole of the doctrine of salvation and the framework of the works of grace.
topics.takeaway: The order of salvation is the logical order of the works of grace by which the believer is brought from death to life, from election to glorification.

ideas: Salvation is the work of God, accomplished in Christ and applied by the Spirit, and received by faith.
The order of salvation runs from the election to the glorification, the works of grace by which the believer is made alive.
Justification is the forensic declaration of righteousness on the ground of the imputed righteousness of Christ, by faith alone.
Sanctification is the progressive making holy, and glorification is the final perfection in the likeness of Christ.
summary.connections: The doctrine of salvation is the application of the work of Christ to the sinner; it is the ground of the Christian's assurance and of the Church's witness, and it flows directly from the person and work of Christ.
summary.progression: Having seen the application of the work of Christ to the sinner, the programme turns to the community in which the saved are gathered: the doctrine of the Church.

modules.title: Ecclesiology: The Doctrine of the Church
modules.divider_intro: The nature, marks, government, ordinances, worship, discipline and mission of the body of Christ.

intro.discipline: Ecclesiology is the doctrine of the Church: its nature, its marks, its government, its ministries, its ordinances, its worship, its discipline, and its mission. It treats the community in which the saved are gathered and in which the work of the redemption is applied and displayed.
intro.context: The Church is the body of Christ, the temple of the Holy Spirit, and the family of God. The New Testament presents the Church as the community of the redeemed, gathered by the Spirit around the word and the ordinances, and sent into the world as the witness of the gospel.
intro.relevance: The doctrine of the Church is the ground of the Christian's communal life and of the Church's witness. It answers the questions of what the Church is, how it is governed, and how it is to live and to witness in the world.
intro.focus: To understand the nature, marks, government, ordinances, worship, discipline and mission of the Church as the body of Christ.

topics.title: The Nature and Definition of the Church
topics.explanation: The Church is the body of Christ, the community of the redeemed, gathered by the Spirit around the word and the ordinances (1 Cor 12:27; Eph 1:22-23). It is at once a spiritual reality — the invisible body of the elect — and a visible community — the congregation of believers on earth. The Church is the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 3:16), the family of God (Eph 2:19), and the bride of Christ (Rev 19:7). The nature of the Church is to be the community of the redeemed, in which the word is preached, the ordinances are administered, and the work of the redemption is applied and displayed.
concepts: The Church as the body of Christ
The invisible body of the elect and the visible community
The Church as the temple of the Spirit and the family of God
The community of the redeemed around the word and the ordinances
topics.context: The doctrine of the Church is the ground of the Christian's communal life and of the Church's witness.
topics.takeaway: The Church is the body of Christ — the community of the redeemed gathered by the Spirit around the word and the ordinances.

topics.title: The Unity, Holiness and Catholicity of the Church
topics.explanation: The Church is one, holy, and catholic — the three attributes confessed in the Nicene Creed. The unity of the Church is the oneness of the body of Christ, the ground of which is the one Spirit, the one Lord, and the one baptism (Eph 4:4-6). The holiness of the Church is the moral and spiritual character of the body, set apart for God and marked by the holiness of its members. The catholicity of the Church is its universality — it is not confined to one place or one age but extends over the whole world and the whole of history. The three attributes are the ground of the Church's self-understanding and of its ecumenical witness.

The holiness: the moral and spiritual character of the body
The catholicity: the universality of the Church
The ground of the Church's self-understanding and ecumenical witness
topics.context: The attributes of the Church are confessed in the Nicene Creed and are the ground of the Church's self-understanding.
topics.takeaway: The Church is one, holy and catholic — the attributes confessed in the Creed and the ground of the Church's self-understanding.

topics.title: The Visible and Invisible Church
topics.explanation: The distinction between the visible and the invisible Church is the distinction between the Church as the visible community of professed believers on earth, and the Church as the invisible body of the elect known only to God. The visible Church includes both the genuine believers and the professed believers who are not yet truly converted; the invisible Church includes only the elect, the true believers. The distinction is the ground of the Church's discipline and of its hope: the visible Church is the community in which the ordinances are administered, and the invisible Church is the body of the redeemed that will be perfected in the age to come. The two are not two churches but two aspects of the one Church.
concepts: The visible Church: the community of professed believers
The invisible Church: the body of the elect
The ground of the Church's discipline and of its hope
Two aspects of the one Church, not two churches
topics.context: The distinction between the visible and the invisible Church is the ground of the Church's discipline and of its hope.
topics.takeaway: The visible and the invisible Church are two aspects of the one Church — the community of professed believers and the body of the elect.

topics.title: The Government of the Church
topics.explanation: The government of the Church is the ordering of the community for the administration of the word, the ordinances, and the discipline. The Scripture presents several forms of government: the episcopal (government by the bishop), the presbyterian (government by the elders or presbyters), and the congregational (government by the congregation). The Reformed tradition affirms the presbyterian form, in which the elders (both teaching and ruling) govern the congregation under the headship of Christ. The government of the Church is to be ordered for the good of the community and the glory of God, and it is always under the lordship of Christ, the head of the Church.

The Reformed affirmation of the presbyterian form
The elders: the teaching and the ruling
The government under the lordship of Christ, the head
topics.context: The forms of church government are to be ordered for the good of the community and the glory of God, under the headship of Christ.
topics.takeaway: The Church is governed by its elders under the headship of Christ, ordered for the good of the community and the glory of God.

topics.title: The Ministries of the Church
topics.explanation: The ministries of the Church are the offices by which the community is built up and the work of the redemption is applied. The Scripture presents the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the pastors and the teachers (Eph 4:11) as the fivefold ministry given to the Church for its equipping. The apostolic ministry was foundational and ceased with the close of the canonical age; the other ministries continue in the Church. The ministry of the pastor is the preaching of the word, the administration of the ordinances, and the shepherding of the flock. The doctrine of the ministries is the ground of the Church's order and of the equipping of the saints for the work of the ministry.

The cessation of the apostolic and prophetic ministries
The ministry of the pastor: preaching, ordinances, shepherding
The equipping of the saints for the work of the ministry
topics.context: The doctrine of the ministries is the ground of the Church's order and of the equipping of the saints.
topics.takeaway: The ministries of the Church are the offices by which the community is built up and the saints are equipped for the work of the ministry.

topics.title: The Doctrine of Baptism
topics.explanation: Baptism is the ordinance of the New Testament in which the believer is buried with Christ and raised with him, and is incorporated into the body of Christ (Rom 6:3-5; 1 Cor 12:13). It is the sign and seal of the covenant of grace, and it is the entrance-ordinance into the visible Church. The doctrine of baptism is to be held in balance: it is not the means of the salvation but the sign of the salvation already accomplished in Christ; it is to be administered to the believer and to the children of believers; and it is to be administered once, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The modes of baptism (sprinkling and immersion) are a matter of practice, not of doctrine.

The burial and the raising with Christ
The entrance-ordinance into the visible Church
The administration to the believer and the children of believers
topics.context: The doctrine of baptism is to be held in balance: it is the sign of the salvation, not the means of it.
topics.takeaway: Baptism is the sign and seal of the covenant of grace, the burial and raising with Christ, and the entrance into the visible Church.

topics.title: The Doctrine of the Lord's Supper
topics.explanation: The Lord's Supper is the ordinance of the New Testament in which the believer partakes of the bread and the cup as the signs and seals of the body and the blood of Christ (1 Cor 11:23-26). It is the memorial of the death of Christ, the proclamation of that death until he comes, and the means by which the believer is fed upon Christ and nourished in the life of grace. The doctrine of the Lord's Supper is to be held in balance: the bread and the cup are not changed into the body and the blood of Christ (against the Roman Catholic transubstantiation) nor are they merely symbolic (against the purely memorialist view); they are the signs and seals of the real presence of Christ by the Spirit. The ordinance is to be administered to the believers who have been examined and found worthy.

The signs and seals of the body and the blood of Christ
The real presence of Christ by the Spirit

topics.context: The doctrine of the Lord's Supper was defined at the Reformation against the Roman Catholic transubstantiation and the Zwinglian memorialism.
topics.takeaway: The Lord's Supper is the sign and seal of the real presence of Christ by the Spirit, the memorial of his death and the means of the believer's nourishment.

topics.title: Sacraments and Ordinances: A Comparative Study
topics.explanation: The Roman Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions differ in their number and their understanding of the sacraments. The Roman Catholic Church affirms seven sacraments; the Orthodox Church affirms the same; the Protestant traditions affirm two ordinances — baptism and the Lord's Supper. The difference is not merely numerical but theological: the Roman Catholic and Orthodox traditions understand the sacraments as the means of the grace ex opere operato (by the work worked), while the Protestant traditions understand the ordinances as the signs and seals of the grace received by faith. The comparative study is to be held in the light of the Scripture and the confession of the faith, and it is to be conducted in a spirit of ecumenical charity.

The two ordinances of the Protestant traditions

topics.context: The comparative study of the sacraments is to be held in the light of the Scripture and conducted in a spirit of ecumenical charity.
topics.takeaway: The traditions differ in the number and the understanding of the sacraments; the Protestant understanding is that of the signs and seals of the grace received by faith.

topics.title: The Worship of the Church
topics.explanation: The worship of the Church is the assembly of the community in which the word is preached, the ordinances are administered, and the people of God give thanks and praise to the triune God. The worship of the Church is governed by the regulative principle — that which is not appointed by the word of God is not to be added to the worship (Deut 12:32; 1 Cor 14:40). The elements of the worship are the preaching of the word, the singing of the psalms and hymns, the prayer, and the administration of the ordinances. The worship of the Church is the ground of the Christian's devotion and of the Church's witness to the world, and it is the chief work of the community.

The regulative principle of the worship
The elements: the word, the song, the prayer, the ordinances
The worship as the chief work of the community
topics.context: The doctrine of the worship is governed by the regulative principle and is the chief work of the community.
topics.takeaway: The worship of the Church is the assembly in which the word is preached and the ordinances are administered, governed by the regulative principle.

topics.title: The Discipline of the Church
topics.explanation: The discipline of the Church is the process by which the community maintains the purity of the body and the honour of the name of Christ. It includes the correction of the offending member, the excommunication of the impenitent, and the restoration of the repentant. The Scripture commands the discipline (Matt 18:15-17; 1 Cor 5:1-13; 2 Thess 3:14-15), and it is the ground of the purity of the body and of the honour of the ordinances. The discipline is to be exercised in a spirit of love and of patience, with the goal of the restoration of the offender and the preservation of the purity of the community. The doctrine of the discipline is the ground of the Church's holiness and of its witness.
